t: Can You Afford The Patience Your Business Needs To Grow?
d: Most African small businesses close within five years. Here is why founders who can afford to wait survive, and how to build that patience yourself.
b: Every year, thousands of Nigerians resign from paid jobs, gather their savings and open a restaurant in Wuse, a boutique in Lekki or a logistics company in Onitsha. Most of them expect the business to pay its own bills within six months and give them a comfortable stream of income within one year. When that does not happen, many close shop, sell the equipment at a loss and decide that the business is not for them. For many of these young, vibrant Nigerians, the idea was sound. What ran out first was TIME. A business needs time to find its customers, fix its prices, learn what sells and survive its first bad season. That period of waiting, learning and adjusting is what we mean by patience in business. Most people do not know that patience has a price. Someone has to pay the rent, the staff and the founder's own living costs while the business finds its feet. Founders who cannot pay it are often forced to quit before the business has had a fair chance. The Data Is the Proof A survival rate is the share of new businesses still operating after a given number of years. Across the world, survival rates for new businesses are low, and the African figures are harsh. Where What the Data Shows Time Frame Source Africa (survey of Nigerian MSMEs) About 80% of small businesses fail Within 5 years Kippa MSME Report, 2022 Kenya About 46% of small businesses closed Within the first year Kenya National Bureau of Statistics MSME Survey, 2016 South Africa Over 70% of small and medium businesses fold Within 5 to 7 years Africa's Public Service Delivery and Performance Review, 2019 Put simply, if ten people in Lagos opened businesses this year, the data suggests only about two would still be operating five years from now. More often than not, those two are the ones who could afford to wait. Why Some Founders Can Wait and Others Cannot Think of patience as a cushion. This cushion is the set of resources outside the business that keeps a founder standing while the business is still weak. We have listed the most common cushions below. Cushion 1: A Family That Can Absorb Failure A founder from a rich or middle-class home can fail and try again. If the first business closes, they move back into the family house or get a family apartment. A parent can offer to fund the second attempt, and family friends become the first customers. Research published by the NBER, based in the United States, found that people who run incorporated businesses tend to come from higher-income families. A founder without this cushion often gets only one attempt, and first attempts are where the most costly lessons are learned. Cushion 2: A Spouse Who Earns and Believes When a husband or wife has a steady source of income, essential household costs like school fees, food and rent are covered. The founder can go without a salary for a year or more and put every naira of profit back into the business. The support runs deeper than money. A spouse who says, "I want you to try again," after a bad quarter gives the founder room to think clearly. A supportive spouse brings calm in the middle of a turbulent storm. Cushion 3: A Salary That Still Comes In Keeping a job while building a business is often mocked as a lack of commitment, yet a study in the Academy of Management Journal found that founders who kept their day jobs while starting their businesses were about a third less likely to fail than those who quit to go full time. A salary buys time to test the idea, find paying customers and make mistakes cheaply. Cushion 4: Access to Credit When Cash Runs Short Credit here means more than a bank loan. It includes a supplier who lets you take goods today and pay in thirty days, a cooperative society, an ajo or esusu contribution group, or a relative who lends without interest. The founder who can borrow cheaply survives a bad month. The founder whose only option is a high-interest loan app often sinks deeper with every repayment. Cushion 5: Emotional Safety In many of our communities, failure is public. People discuss it at family meetings, in church and in WhatsApp groups. A founder who fears that shame will either quit early or hide problems until they are too big to fix. Research shows that a founder who feels safe can admit a mistake early, change direction and keep going. This cushion functions as an emotional safety net, keeping founders steady while they handle the many moving parts of a business. That safety can come from a spouse, a mentor, or a community of fellow business owners. The Silent Killer: When the Business Becomes the Family Purse One of the most common and least discussed reasons small businesses die in Africa is the founder using company money to meet personal and family obligations. School fees are due in September. A parent needs a hospital bill paid. There is a burial in the village, a wedding with its aso ebi, a sibling's rent. The founder has no personal cushion, so the money comes from the only place it can: the business account. This is called Black Tax. When Black Tax enters a business, it takes away the ability to run the business efficiently and reinvest in what matters most. A 2024 study of Kenyan business owners found that about 1 in 3 founders faced strong pressure to share income with relatives, and those under pressure were less likely to invest extra cash in their businesses. Another study of Ghanaian businesses listed diversion of business funds among the most frequent causes of failure, with loans meant for operations spent on private cars and private buildings. How to Buy Patience You Were Not Born With If you did not inherit any of the five cushions above, you can still build some of them before and during the life of your business. Separate the money. Open a business account and never pay personal bills from it. Pay yourself a fixed salary, however small, and live on it. Build a personal runway of six to twelve months of living costs before leaving paid work. Keep your job or another income for as long as you can while you test the idea. Start small. Rent less, hire slowly and share space where possible. Talk to your family early about what the business can and cannot carry. Build credit relationships before you need them, with suppliers, cooperatives and your bank. Plan for years, not months. Budget as if profit will take three years to arrive. What You Must Never Forget Business rewards the people who stay long enough to learn. It takes time, effort, finance and mental agility to run and build a successful business. Before you resign, sign a lease or take a loan, ask yourself if you can afford the patience the business requires. Traction Outsourcing Limited helps founders and business owners across Nigeria build the structure that lets them afford the patience their business needs. We develop business plans with realistic timelines, set up financial and management systems that keep personal and business money apart, and provide HR outsourcing so young companies are not weighed down by a full payroll too early. If your business needs more time than you can currently afford, book a call with our team and let us help you plan for the long road. Why do most small businesses in Nigeria fail within five years? Data from the Kippa MSME Report shows about 80% of small businesses in Nigeria fail within five years. The most common reason is not a bad idea but running out of time: founders often cannot personally afford to keep paying their bills long enough for the business to become profitable. What is a 'cushion' in the context of starting a business? A cushion is a resource outside the business that keeps a founder financially and emotionally stable while the business is still weak. Common cushions include family wealth, a working spouse, a salary from another job, access to affordable credit and emotional support from family or a community. What is Black Tax and how does it affect a business? Black Tax refers to the pressure on a founder to use business income to cover personal and family financial obligations, such as school fees, medical bills or family ceremonies. A 2024 study found that about 1 in 3 Kenyan founders faced strong pressure to share income with relatives, and founders under that pressure were less likely to reinvest in their businesses. How can a founder build patience if they do not have family wealth to fall back on? Founders can build their own cushion by separating personal and business finances, paying themselves a small fixed salary, saving six to twelve months of living costs before quitting a job, keeping other income for as long as possible, starting small, and building credit relationships with suppliers or cooperatives before they are needed.

t: When Will You Fire That Staff?
d: He meets his targets, refuses every Performance Improvement Plan, and answers to nobody but you. Here is how to decide whether a high performer who defies authority should be trained or let go, and how to do it right.
b: Almost every company has one staff, and your business has had this one for about 5 years. He started with you when you were still small. He was among the first people you hired, back when the office was two rooms in Lagos Mainland and salaries were paid after a tense conversation at the end of every month. He knows where every file is kept, which client prefers a phone call to an email, and exactly how the business survived its hardest year. Every quarter, he meets his targets, and sometimes surpasses them. Last year, your HR manager placed him on a Performance Improvement Plan. A PIP is a programme that sets out what must change in a staff member's conduct or output, how that change will be measured, and the date by which it must happen. This staff refused to sign it or engage in it. This year, 3 months ago, your HR had to bring up another PIP. He called it an insult in front of the entire staff. When his line manager followed up, he went behind the line manager and went straight to you. He knows you very well and even considers you a friend. Yet, he is secretly destroying the culture your HR manager was employed to build. In the past 2 years, 5 amazing staff have resigned and they stated that he was the reason they had to go. The remaining staff treat him like a demi-god, and they are always careful what not to say around him. You know he is hurting your company's long term growth but you keep postponing every meeting your HR manager scheduled to discuss his issues. So, here is the real question: When will you fire that staff? Why This Kind of Staff Survives Three things usually protect a staff like this, and none of them tells you whether the person is good for the business. The first is the target. Leaders look at a sales figure or a list of completed projects and treat it as final proof of value. A target measures output. It says nothing about what that output cost the people around it, or who quietly carried the work that made the numbers possible. The second is tenure. Long service builds loyalty and knowledge, and both are worth something. In many Nigerian workplaces, though, years of service slowly turn into an unofficial rank that sits outside the organogram. On paper the staff reports to a manager. In practice they report to nobody. The third, and the hardest to say out loud, is closeness to the top. When a staff is known to be friends with the CEO, every manager below does a quick calculation before correcting them, and most decide the risk is not worth it. The CEO believes the managers are in charge. The managers believe the CEO has taken sides. The staff sits comfortably in the gap between those two beliefs, a gap our article on when the CEO becomes the weak link covers in more depth. What Keeping Them Actually Costs Keeping a high performer who misbehaves feels like a sensible commercial decision. The research points the other way. Research from the talent management firm Cornerstone found that good employees became 54 percent more likely to quit when just one toxic person joined a team of 20. A study published in MIT Sloan Management Review, which analysed 1.4 million employee reviews, found that a toxic culture was 10.4 times more powerful than pay in predicting whether people left a company, with feeling disrespected listed among its main ingredients. Then there is the wider cost of people who stay but stop trying. Gallup's 2026 global workplace report found that only 20 percent of employees worldwide were engaged at work in 2025, and it put the cost of that lost productivity at around $10 trillion. In our experience at Traction Outsourcing, few things drain engagement faster than watching one person break every rule and face no consequence. Bring that home to a 30-person business in Abuja or Lagos. Losing two good officers means recruitment costs, weeks of empty desks, new staff learning on the job, and client relationships that walk out of the door with the people who built them. The staff who "meets targets" may be costing you far more than their targets bring in. Fire or Train? A Practical Guide Not every difficult staff should be let go. Most performance problems can be fixed, and firing too quickly carries its own costs. The useful test is to separate skill from will. A skill problem means the person cannot yet do what the role needs, and training usually solves it. A will problem means the person can do it but refuses, and once a fair process has been offered and rejected, training has nothing left to fix. Type of Staff What You Notice Fire or Train? Why The struggling new hire Mistakes, slow output, asks many questions Train Early mistakes usually point to missing onboarding, not a bad hire The willing but outdated veteran Loyal and respectful, but struggling with new tools or systems Train The attitude is right and the skills can be updated The low performer with a good attitude Tries hard, accepts feedback, misses targets Train, with a clear deadline Give a structured PIP; if there is no progress by the deadline, move to exit The staff in the wrong role Poor results in one role, strong signs of ability elsewhere Redeploy and train The person may be fine and the role may be wrong The burnt-out former star Once excellent, now withdrawn and slipping Train and support first Find out what changed before deciding anything The low performer with a bad attitude Misses targets and resists correction Fire, after due process There is neither output nor willingness to build on The high performer who defies authority Meets targets, refuses PIPs, undermines managers Fire, after due process The damage to the team outweighs the numbers, as the research shows The staff involved in fraud, theft or harassment Serious misconduct, confirmed by investigation Fire Keeping them exposes the business to legal and reputational risk Letting Go the Right Way in Nigeria Once the decision is made, how you carry it out matters as much as the decision. A careless exit can turn a staff problem into a court case. Document everything. Every PIP, query letter, warning and refusal should be written down, dated and filed. A pattern on paper protects you far better than a pattern everyone simply remembers. Get the CEO to agree the process in advance and then step back from the individual case. If the friendship is the reason previous efforts failed, the CEO's most useful contribution is to back the managers publicly and let the process run. Give a fair hearing. Where you are dismissing a staff for misconduct, Nigerian labour law expects the employee to be given an opportunity to defend themselves before the decision is taken. In practice, that means a query, a written response and a proper disciplinary panel. Respect notice periods. Section 11 of the Labour Act sets minimum notice by length of service: one day for under three months, one week for three months to two years, two weeks for two to five years, and one month for over five years. Many contracts set longer periods, and salary can be paid in lieu of notice. A nine-year staff is owed at least one month, or more if their contract says so. Pay every final entitlement , including salary to date, unused leave and any gratuity their contract provides. The National Industrial Court can award damages where termination is found to be wrongful, so speak with an employment lawyer before any sensitive exit. Our guide to employee leave and compensation in Nigeria covers what a fair final settlement should include. When one staff can cancel a PIP by walking into the CEO's office, you are looking at more than one person's attitude. What You Need To Know Reporting lines, disciplinary policy and the authority of managers have all been quietly overwritten. Remove that staff without fixing those things, and the next untouchable is only a few years away. This is why the conversation about letting someone go often leads to a bigger one about how the business is structured. Traction Outsourcing Limited helps organisations across Nigeria restructure the way they are run : redrawing the organogram so reporting lines are real, defining roles and delegated authority, building performance management and disciplinary systems that apply to everyone, and supporting leaders through the hard people decisions that follow. If a staff in your business has grown bigger than your structure, book a call with our team and let us help you put the structure back in charge. Further Reading: When the CEO Is the Weak Link , Accountability in Business: How to Hold Your Staff Accountable Without Losing Them , Organizational Design Model as a Tool for Effective Corporate Restructuring . When should you fire a high-performing staff member? A high performer should be considered for dismissal when they consistently defy authority: refusing performance improvement plans, undermining their manager, or damaging team culture, even while meeting targets. Research shows a single toxic team member can make good employees far more likely to quit, and can be up to 10 times more powerful than pay in predicting turnover. The commercial value of their output rarely outweighs the cost of losing the people around them. How do you know if a staff member should be trained instead of fired? Separate skill from will. If the person cannot yet do what the role needs but is willing to learn and accepts feedback, training with a clear, time-bound Performance Improvement Plan usually solves it. If the person can do the job but refuses to change their conduct after a fair process has been offered, training has nothing left to fix and the case moves toward a disciplinary exit. What notice period is required to dismiss a staff member in Nigeria? Section 11 of the Nigerian Labour Act sets minimum notice periods based on length of service: one day for under three months of service, one week for three months to two years, two weeks for two to five years, and one month for over five years of service. Many employment contracts set longer periods than this minimum, and notice can be paid in lieu rather than worked.

t: The Norman Door Test: Applying Design Thinking to How Your Business Actually Runs
d: A flat plate on a door you have to pull defeats people daily, and nobody designed it to embarrass them. Here is what design theorist Don Norman's work reveals about the doors your staff and clients keep hesitating at.
b: Walk into almost any office building in Abuja or Lagos and you will find at least one door that defeats people daily. It has a flat metal plate at chest height, the kind that only makes sense on a door you push, yet the door needs to be pulled. Visitors slow down, hesitate, push anyway, bounce off it, then pull sheepishly while glancing around to see who noticed. Nobody designed that door to embarrass people. It simply gave them no clue about what to do, and they filled the gap with a guess that happened to be wrong. The design theorist Don Norman noticed this exact failure everywhere he looked, so often that doors like this now carry his name in design circles. He built an entire body of work, most famously the book "The Design of Everyday Things," around a single idea that sounds almost too simple to matter: when people fail to use something correctly, the fault rarely belongs to them. It belongs to whoever built the thing and assumed the user would figure it out. That idea, once you notice it, is impossible to unsee in how many Nigerian businesses are run. What Don Norman Actually Argued Don Norman's design thinking rests on a handful of principles that translate directly into business life. A signifier is a cue that tells a person what action to take, a flat plate for push, a handle for pull. Feedback confirms that an action worked, a light that turns on, a message that says received. Mapping is the natural link between a control and what it does, a switch positioned near the device it operates. A conceptual model is the mental picture a person builds of how something works before they even try it. When any of these go missing, people do not fail because they are careless. They fail because they were never given anything to work with, and they had to invent their own logic on the spot. Don Norman's argument was that good design removes the guessing entirely. A business, at its core, is also a designed system, and it fails or succeeds by the same rules. Nobody designs a door to embarrass the person walking through it. They just forget to tell them which way to push. The Staff Version of the Norman Door Picture a new front desk hire at a consulting firm in Abuja, three days into the job, facing an angry walk-in client for the first time. Nobody handed her a written procedure for this. She was told to use her initiative, so she does, escalating the complaint to the wrong department. Her manager later queries her for poor judgement, without pausing to ask whether the judgement was ever hers to have in the first place. This is a Norman door wearing a staff badge. The business gave her no signifier, no signpost for what to do when a client walked in upset, and expected the correct action to occur to her naturally. When it did not, she carried the blame that belonged to the missing structure. Multiply this across every new hire and the pattern becomes visible: an owner growing frustrated that staff "cannot think," staff growing quietly resentful of being punished for something nobody taught them, and a business that keeps hiring for common sense instead of building the system that would make common sense unnecessary. The fix costs far less than the damage it prevents. A one page escalation chart pinned near the front desk, a short onboarding pack that walks through the first ten situations a new hire will actually meet, a checklist for the tasks that repeat every week. None of this is complicated, and it is exactly the kind of documentation structured staff training is built to produce. It simply replaces a blank wall with a signifier, the flat plate that tells a person which way to push. The Client Version of the Norman Door The same failure happens on the other side of the counter. A client visits an office to discuss a service and finds no one has told them where to sit, who to ask for, or what happens first, the conversation or the paperwork. A job applicant submits a CV and is left to guess whether silence means rejection or simply a slow process. A client who has just signed an agreement is not told whether to expect an invoice first or a call to schedule a deposit, so they phone the office repeatedly just to find out what comes next. None of these clients are being unreasonable. They are standing in front of a Norman door, one built from silence instead of steel, and they are doing what anyone does at a door with no signifier: guessing, hesitating, or walking away. A business that wants to keep a client through the full length of a transaction has to remove that guesswork at every step, a confirmation message after every stage, a printed or emailed next-steps sheet, and front-of-house staff who have been properly briefed to say exactly where a new visitor should go before they even have to ask. Running the Norman Door Test Before assuming a mistake was carelessness, on either side of the business, it is worth running a quick test. Can a new staff member complete this task correctly without first asking a colleague what to do? Can a client move to the next step without calling the office to confirm it? If ten different people faced this same point in the process, would most of them get it right on the first try, or would most of them hesitate the way visitors hesitate at a door with no signifier? If the honest answer points to hesitation, the problem is not the person standing at that door. It is the door. How Traction Outsourcing Helps You Fix the Doors This is the work behind the work. Startup structuring builds the signifiers a growing business does not yet have, the org charts, escalation paths, and process documents that tell every new hire exactly which way to push. Business advisory helps founders further along find the doors that have been silently confusing staff and clients for years, the ones everyone has simply learned to push against out of habit. Once the structure exists on paper, corporate training makes sure it actually reaches the people who need it, and staff outsourcing puts trained people in the roles where a missing signifier costs the most, the front desk, the first client call, the first week of a new hire's job. The Practical Takeaway Don Norman's real gift to business owners is permission to stop blaming people for problems that structure created. Assuming that staff or clients will simply know what to do is the fastest route to job dissatisfaction, owner frustration, and quiet inefficiency, because it hands the outcome of every interaction over to guesswork and hopes for the best. The businesses that grow with less friction are usually the ones that have gone through their own processes, from the first day of onboarding to the last line of an invoice, and replaced every unmarked door with a clear signifier. Staff stop guessing. Clients stop calling to ask what happens next. Everyone, on both sides of the business, already knows which way to push. Further Reading: What Is Structure in Business? , Why Every Nigerian SME Needs an Employee Handbook , Why Nigerian Businesses Are Investing in Staff Training . What is a "Norman door" in a business context? A Norman door is named after design theorist Don Norman, who wrote about doors so poorly designed that people cannot tell whether to push or pull them. In a business, a Norman door is any process, staff task, or client interaction that gives no clear signal for what to do next, forcing people to guess and often guess wrong. Why does Don Norman say the user is rarely at fault? Don Norman's core argument in "The Design of Everyday Things" is that when people fail to use something correctly, the fault usually belongs to whoever designed it and assumed the correct action would be obvious. Businesses that blame staff for "not thinking" or clients for "not reading instructions" are often missing a structural problem, not a people problem. How do I know if my business has a Norman door problem? Run a simple test: can a new staff member complete a given task correctly without first asking a colleague, and can a client move to the next step without calling the office to confirm it? If most people would hesitate or guess wrong, the process is missing a clear signifier, and that is a structural gap rather than a training failure alone. What is the fastest way to fix a Norman door in a growing business? Start with the highest-traffic points of confusion: a one-page escalation chart for front desk staff, a short onboarding pack covering the first situations a new hire will meet, and a confirmation message or next-steps sheet for clients after every stage of a transaction. None of these require major investment, only clear documentation of what already exists.

t: Upselling vs Cross-Selling: Exploring Sales Options for Your Business
d: The woman selling shoes who suggests the better sole is upselling. The suya seller who asks about extra pepper and a cold drink is cross-selling. Here is how to know which fits your business.
b: Walk into any market in Lagos, Kano, or Enugu and you will find both techniques already at play, even if the traders have never heard the terms. The woman selling shoes who convinces you to take the version with the better sole is upselling. The man selling suya who asks if you want extra pepper and a cold drink with that is cross-selling. Understanding the difference, and knowing which one fits your business, can change how much every customer is worth to you. What is Upselling? Upselling means guiding a customer toward a higher-value version of what they already intend to buy. The customer walks in wanting a laptop with 4GB of RAM. The salesperson shows them the 8GB model, explains it will serve them for years instead of months, and the customer leaves with a better product and a bigger bill. Upselling works because it builds on a decision the customer has already made. You are not creating a new need, you are expanding one that already exists. Consider a furniture business in Abuja. A customer comes in for a simple wooden dining chair. The salesperson points to a cushioned version with better joinery and a two-year warranty. The additional cost is modest set against the added comfort and durability, and many customers will take it once the value is spelled out clearly. A phone retailer in Ikeja sees this constantly. A customer asks for the 128GB version of a popular smartphone. The salesperson shows the 256GB model, and points out that photos and videos fill a phone faster than most buyers expect, especially with how much time is spent on WhatsApp status and Instagram Reels. The price difference is a fraction of the phone's total cost, and framed against running out of storage in six months, it becomes an easy decision. What is Cross-Selling? Cross-selling introduces a related product that complements the original purchase. The phone shop that sells a smartphone and then offers a screen protector, a case, and earphones is cross-selling. None of these items replace the phone. They round it off. A tailoring business offers a strong example. A client comes in for a native attire for a wedding. The tailor suggests matching accessories, a cap, or a bag to complete the look. The client was not planning to buy those items, but they fit naturally into what is already being purchased. A restaurant in Port Harcourt shows the same instinct at work. A table orders jollof rice and grilled chicken, and the waiter asks if they would like chilled zobo or a bottle of wine to go with it. Neither drink changes what was already ordered. It simply completes the meal, and because the suggestion arrives as part of good service rather than a sales pitch, most tables say yes without a second thought. A Quick Reference by Industry Industry Product Type Natural Lean Why Fashion and tailoring Ready-to-wear and made-to-order clothing Cross-selling Complementary items such as accessories and footwear complete an outfit Real estate Residential and commercial property Upselling Buyers already compare tiers by size, finishing, and location Food and hospitality Restaurant meals, event catering Cross-selling Drinks, sides, and desserts pair naturally with a meal Automobile sales Vehicles and after-sales service Upselling Buyers weigh trims, engine capacity, and added features Electronics and gadgets Phones, laptops, appliances Both, evenly Accessories cross-sell well; storage and specification upgrades upsell well Beauty and wellness Skincare, spa, salon services Cross-selling Treatments and products are bought as sets, not single items Financial services Loans, insurance, savings products Upselling Higher tiers of cover or credit are compared against a base offer The Psychology Behind It in African Markets African consumers, and Nigerian consumers in particular, tend to respond more readily to cross-selling than upselling, and the reason sits in how buying decisions are made. Purchases here are rarely private transactions between a buyer and a price tag. They carry a social weight. A wedding outfit is judged alongside the shoes and the accessories that go with it. A meal at an event is remembered as a full experience, drinks and all. Bundling fits naturally into a culture where value is measured by completeness, not by the specification sheet of a single item. Upselling asks a customer to justify spending more on the same thing, which invites second-guessing and comparison with what a neighbour or relative paid. Cross-selling avoids that comparison because it is framed as care rather than upsell: you will need this along with that, rather than pay more for a better version of this. This is why food and hospitality, fashion, and beauty services see cross-selling succeed with far less resistance than industries like real estate or vehicles, where upselling works because the purchase itself is already a public statement of status and buyers expect tiers. Traders who understand this rarely announce it as strategy. They simply ask the right question at the right moment, and the customer walks away feeling looked after rather than sold to. That instinct, once businesses formalise it into a deliberate policy across staff and outlets, is where the real revenue sits. The best salesmanship rarely feels like selling. It feels like being looked after. Common Mistakes Businesses Make With Both Upselling before trust is established. Pushing the premium option in the first thirty seconds of an interaction, before a customer has decided the business is even worth buying from, reads as pressure rather than guidance. The upsell lands better once the customer has already committed to the base purchase. Cross-selling items that do not actually relate. Suggesting a completely unrelated product just to raise the bill breaks the trust cross-selling depends on. The suggestion has to genuinely complete what the customer is already buying, not simply add to it. Treating it as a script instead of a judgment call. A rigid line repeated to every customer regardless of what they are buying or how they are behaving sounds robotic and gets tuned out. Staff need to understand the principle well enough to apply it naturally, not recite it. Not knowing when to stop. A customer who has already said no once and is asked again, or offered a third add-on after declining the first two, starts to feel handled rather than helped. Reading that moment correctly is part of the skill, and it is exactly the kind of judgment that structured sales training builds in a team. How Traction Outsourcing Helps You Build a Winning Sales Policy Knowing the difference between upselling and cross-selling is the easy part. Building it into how a whole team actually sells, consistently, across every shift and every outlet, is where most businesses struggle. That is where Corporate Trainings from Traction Outsourcing Limited comes in. We work with sales and front-line teams to turn this from a vague instinct held by your best salesperson into a documented, trainable policy every member of staff can apply with confidence. For businesses still figuring out which approach fits their pricing structure, product mix, and customer base, our Business Advisory team helps map that out before a single naira is spent on training. And because a sales policy is only as strong as the people delivering it, our Staff Outsourcing and HR Management service ensures the salespeople you hire in the first place are suited to the kind of relationship-driven selling that wins in Nigerian markets. The Practical Takeaway Neither approach replaces the other, and the strongest businesses use both depending on what is being sold and to whom. A business selling status-driven, infrequent purchases should build a clear tier structure and train staff to upsell with confidence. A business selling frequent, experience-driven purchases should build a cross-selling habit into every transaction, because the smaller add-ons compound fast across volume. The businesses that grow quietly are usually the ones that have made this distinction without ever needing to name it, often with the support of a business advisory partner who can help structure the policy across a whole team. Further Reading: What Is Traction in Business? , Profit vs Cashflow: The King of Business , Why Nigerian Businesses Train Staff . What is the difference between upselling and cross-selling? Upselling guides a customer toward a higher-value version of the product they already intend to buy, such as a laptop with more storage. Cross-selling introduces a related, complementary product alongside the original purchase, such as a phone case sold with a new phone. Upselling expands a decision the customer has already made; cross-selling adds a decision they had not yet considered. Why does cross-selling work better than upselling in Nigerian and African markets? Purchases in African markets often carry social weight and are judged as a complete experience rather than a single item, so bundling related products feels natural rather than like a sales tactic. Upselling asks a customer to justify spending more on the same thing, which invites comparison with what others paid, while cross-selling is framed as care, offering something that pairs naturally with what is already being bought. Which businesses should focus on upselling? Businesses selling status-driven or infrequent purchases, such as real estate, vehicles, and financial services, tend to see the most success with upselling. Buyers in these categories already compare tiers by size, finishing, features, or coverage, so presenting a higher-value option fits how the decision is already being made. Which businesses should focus on cross-selling? Businesses selling frequent, experience-driven purchases, such as fashion, food and hospitality, and beauty services, tend to see the most success with cross-selling. Customers in these categories buy in sets rather than single items, so complementary add-ons feel like a natural part of the purchase rather than an upsell.

t: Is Your Business Suffering from Sociological Solipsism?
d: When a leader trusts only what happens inside the business and treats every outside voice as noise, the business has crossed into what social scientists call sociological solipsism.
b: Every business leader believes they understand their organisation better than anyone outside it. That belief is healthy, until it hardens into something else. When a leader begins to trust only what happens inside the four walls of the business and treats every outside voice, from customers to market data, as noise, the business has crossed into a condition called Sociological Solipsism. What Is a Solipsistic Business? Solipsism is the notion that reality begins and ends with the self. The term can be traced to ancient Greek, where it is simply described as "the self alone or the self on its own" (Waribugo & Eketu, 2016). Applied to organisations, Sociological Solipsism describes a business that has convinced itself it needs no outside reference point to know what is true, what works, and what its customers want. At Traction Outsourcing Limited, we see this pattern often in our work with growing businesses across Nigeria. A company builds early success on instinct, that instinct hardens into doctrine, and soon the business stops asking whether the world outside still agrees with it. A Solipsistic business is one that treats its own internal culture, opinions, and habits as the only reliable source of truth. Decisions are made by looking only inward rather than both outward and inward. Market research, competitor movement, and customer feedback are acknowledged in meetings but rarely allowed to change anything. The business may not necessarily be arrogant in tone, but it still refuses to let any beneficial data from outside genuinely alter its course. Are You Running a Solipsistic Business? You may be running a Solipsistic business if the following sound familiar: Do you often think that outsiders, including customers and consultants, cannot really understand your business the way you and your team do? When a new employee or partner raises a concern based on outside experience, is the first instinct in the room to explain why "that does not apply here"? Do strategy meetings spend more time confirming what leadership already believes than testing it against fresh information? When sales dip or feedback turns negative, is the explanation almost always about the market being wrong rather than the business missing something? Have you noticed that reports and dashboards seem to always confirm the story leadership already wanted to tell? If two or more of these describe your organisation, Sociological Solipsism may already be shaping how decisions get made. It rarely arrives as a single dramatic moment. It builds slowly, one dismissed suggestion at a time, until the habit of looking outward has quietly disappeared from the business. Core Characteristics of Solipsistic Businesses Internal validation over external verification. Leadership relies on what feels true inside the business rather than what real data confirms. Psychological research on social hierarchy found that a similar pattern shows up among individuals with abundant resources and elevated status, who tend to develop "an individualistic focus on one's own internal states, goals, motivations, and emotions" rather than attending to outside forces (Kraus, Piff, Mendoza-Denton, Rheinschmidt & Keltner, 2012). A business with resources and market dominance can fall into the same trap. Success breeds a quiet confidence that eventually curdles into the belief that the business has nothing left to learn. Dismissal of dissenting voices. New ideas from junior staff, outside consultants, or customers are politely received and quietly ignored. The organisation prizes agreement over challenge, and over time, employees learn that raising outside evidence is a waste of energy. This does not happen because leadership is unkind but happens because disagreement makes meetings slower, and the path of least resistance becomes silence. Founder or leadership worship. Strategy revolves around the instincts of one person or a small inner circle, and their judgement is treated as beyond question. Even when outcomes contradict the original decision, the instinct is to defend the decision rather than revisit it. Resistance to benchmarking. The business avoids comparing itself honestly to competitors or industry standards, often on the reasoning that its situation is too unique for comparison. This reasoning is rarely tested. It simply becomes the accepted explanation whenever someone suggests looking at what other businesses in the same space are doing differently. Feedback loops that only confirm. Surveys, reviews, and reports are designed or interpreted in ways that reinforce what leadership already believes, rather than in ways that could surface uncomfortable truths. A customer satisfaction survey with only positive response options, for instance, will always deliver good news, whether or not the news is true. Isolation from the wider ecosystem. Solipsistic businesses tend to reduce their engagement with industry bodies, peer networks, and external advisors over time. The fewer outside voices in the room, the easier it becomes to mistake internal agreement for external truth. A business does not usually announce that it has stopped listening. It simply keeps deciding, more confidently each time, using information that stopped updating months or years ago. The Cost of Sociological Solipsism A business trapped in this pattern eventually pays for it, and the cost tends to arrive quietly before it arrives loudly. Products stop evolving because the team assumes it already knows what customers want. Talented employees leave when their outside experience is repeatedly waved away, taking with them the very perspective that could have kept the business current. Competitors that stay closer to the market begin to win customers the solipsistic business never saw, because nobody inside the business was watching closely enough to notice the shift. Perhaps most damaging, the organisation loses the early warning signs that would have let it correct course before a small problem became a large one. Complaints that could have been addressed in a week become reputational damage that takes years to repair. A business that only listens to itself eventually finds that the world has moved on without asking permission, and by the time leadership notices, the cost of catching up is far higher than the cost of staying attentive would ever have been. This is precisely the gap that outside HR and management consulting exists to close. Much of the work we do at Traction Outsourcing Limited, whether through recruitment support, workplace culture audits, or strategic advisory, begins with a simple diagnostic question: what does this business believe about itself that the market no longer agrees with? That single question, asked honestly, is often the first step out of sociological solipsism. How to Prevent Sociological Solipsism in the Workplace Build structured channels for outside feedback. Customer surveys, exit interviews, and competitor analysis should not be occasional exercises. They should run continuously and report directly to leadership, not filtered through layers that soften uncomfortable findings. The goal is not more data for its own sake, but data that leadership actually sees in its raw, unedited form. Rotate leadership exposure to the front line. Executives who regularly sit with customer-facing staff, visit markets, and observe operations firsthand are far less likely to mistake internal comfort for external reality. There is no substitute for a leader hearing a complaint directly rather than reading a summary of it three levels removed. Reward dissent, not just agreement. A culture that only promotes people who echo leadership will never surface the concerns that matter. Deliberately create room in meetings for the person willing to say the uncomfortable thing, and make sure that person is not quietly punished for it afterward. Bring in outside expertise on a regular basis. An external partner with no stake in internal politics can see patterns a business cannot see about itself. This is where firms such as Traction Outsourcing Limited add real value. Our work spans HR consulting, workforce management , and management advisory. We help businesses test internal assumptions against what is actually happening in the wider market. We could run a workplace culture audit, for example, which may reveal gaps between how leadership believes the business feels to work in and how employees actually experience it day to day. Bringing in that kind of outside lens on a regular schedule, rather than only during a crisis, gives leadership a standing check against solipsism rather than a one-time correction. Sociological solipsism does not announce itself. It grows quietly inside businesses that have had enough early success to believe they no longer need to look outward. The correction is not complicated, though it does require discipline. It simply requires a leadership team willing to treat outside information as a gift rather than a threat, and a partner willing to keep asking the questions the business has stopped asking itself. To talk about an outside review of your business, call +234 707 870 7777 or email partner@tolnigeria.com . Further Reading: Tall Poppy Syndrome in Business , The Dangers of Proximity to Success , Accountability in Business . What is sociological solipsism in business? Sociological solipsism describes a business that trusts only what happens inside its own walls and treats outside voices, including customers, market data, and industry trends, as noise rather than useful information. Decisions are made by looking inward, and market research or customer feedback is acknowledged but rarely allowed to change anything. What are the signs that a business has become solipsistic? Common signs include dismissing outside concerns as things that "do not apply here," strategy meetings that confirm existing beliefs rather than test them, blaming the market rather than the business when performance dips, feedback surveys designed to only return good news, and shrinking engagement with industry peers and external advisors. What does sociological solipsism cost a business? Products stop evolving because the team assumes it already knows what customers want. Talented employees leave when their outside experience is repeatedly dismissed. Competitors that stay closer to the market win customers the business never saw leaving. Most damaging, the business loses the early warning signs that would have let it correct small problems before they became large, costly ones. How can a business prevent sociological solipsism? Build structured, continuous channels for outside feedback that reach leadership unfiltered, rotate leadership exposure to front-line customer contact, reward employees who raise uncomfortable dissenting views instead of only promoting agreement, and bring in outside expertise on a regular schedule rather than only during a crisis.

t: Setting Up a Winning Team in Your Business
d: A single tree does not make a forest. Here is how Traction Outsourcing approaches talent acquisition, from finding the right people to helping them grow long after they are hired.
b: There is an African proverb that says a single tree does not make a forest. It is a simple line, but it carries a truth every business owner eventually learns. No matter how sharp your vision is or how many hours you put in, your business grows through the people standing beside you. This is why organisations never stop looking for competent professionals to fill important roles and add real value. At Traction Outsourcing Limited, we call this process Talent Acquisition, and we define it as the strategic process of identifying, attracting, and securing the right people to meet a business's current and future workforce needs. Notice the word future. A hiring process that only solves today's problem will leave you scrambling again in a year. The right approach looks ahead. A Lesson on Investing in Potential There is a story in the Christian holy book of Matthew, chapter 25, that captures this idea well. A business owner had to travel, so before he left, he called his staff together and gave each of them a portion of his wealth to manage, based on what he already knew of their strengths. Some were given more, some less. While he was away, the ones who took their responsibility seriously put the resources to work and doubled what they had been given. One person, however, was afraid of losing what was entrusted to him, so he buried it and did nothing with it. When the owner returned, the ones who had grown their portion were praised and given even more responsibility. The one who did nothing lost the little he had. The lesson here is not really about money. It is about potential and what happens when it is nurtured versus when it is left untouched. Talent that is recognised, trusted, and given room to grow will always create value. Talent that is boxed in or ignored will eventually stagnate, no matter how promising it once looked. This mirrors exactly what happens in modern workplaces. Businesses do not grow simply because they hired good people. They grow because they invested in those people afterward. Abilities that go unnoticed or unused are a quiet loss, both for the employee and for the organisation paying their salary every month. The story is never really about the resource itself. It is about what happens to potential once it is trusted with responsibility, and what happens when it is not. Our Approach to Talent Acquisition and Management At Traction Outsourcing Limited, we help businesses find the employees who will still be driving results long after the hiring process is over. Once a candidate is brought on board, we work closely with them to assess their skills and how well they fit the culture of the organisation, then we design development plans that are specific to them, backed by mentorship that builds real confidence. The goal is straightforward. We want your business to have staff who can keep things running smoothly even when you are not physically present, much like the servants who were trusted to manage in their master's absence. Organisations that work with us on this benefit from a well developed talent pool, fewer hiring mistakes, and stronger retention, because their employees feel genuinely supported rather than simply employed. Choosing the Most Suitable Candidate, Not Just the Best One One thing we hold firmly to at Traction Outsourcing Limited is that the best candidate on paper is not always the right candidate for your business. A polished CV, an impressive CGPA, and a list of big company names can catch attention, but none of that guarantees impact in your specific environment. What matters more is suitability. The most suitable candidate is someone whose skills, personality, values, and working style genuinely align with your business's goals, culture, and pace. For growing businesses especially, this kind of fit tends to matter far more than a stack of qualifications, because a person who fits your environment will grow with you, while a person who simply looks good on paper may struggle to settle in at all. A single tree does not make a forest, and no business scales alone. The businesses that grow fastest are the ones that treat talent acquisition as an investment they keep making, not a task they complete once and move on from. Further Reading: How to Find the Best Recruitment Agency in Nigeria , The Real Cost of a Bad Hire in Nigeria , ATH Recruiters . What is talent acquisition? Talent acquisition is the strategic process of identifying, attracting, and securing the right people to meet a business's current and future workforce needs. Unlike a one-off hiring push that only solves today's staffing gap, talent acquisition looks ahead and plans for the roles a business will need to fill as it grows. How is talent acquisition different from recruitment? Recruitment typically focuses on filling an immediate vacancy. Talent acquisition is the broader, longer-term process: it plans for future workforce needs, and it continues after hiring through onboarding, skills assessment, development planning, and mentorship, rather than ending once an offer letter is signed. Why does Traction Outsourcing focus on candidate suitability rather than qualifications alone? A polished CV or an impressive academic record does not guarantee someone will perform well in a specific business environment. Suitability, how well a candidate's skills, personality, values, and working style align with a business's goals and culture, predicts long-term performance and retention more reliably than qualifications alone, particularly for growing businesses. What happens after a candidate is hired through Traction Outsourcing? Once a candidate is brought on board, Traction Outsourcing assesses their skills and cultural fit, designs a development plan specific to them, and backs it with mentorship. The goal is a well developed talent pool, fewer hiring mistakes, and stronger retention, because employees feel genuinely supported rather than simply employed.

t: Organizational Design Model as a Tool for Effective Corporate Restructuring
d: What a chessboard can teach you about corporate structure, and the eight-step model Traction Outsourcing uses to guide effective organizational redesign.
b: Many of us grew up watching a chess board without knowing that its modern design, the one Nathaniel Cooke and Howard Staunton popularized generations ago, was ever a deliberate choice. Yet once you understand the logic behind each move, the whole game changes. A business works the same way. What looks like a random arrangement of departments and job titles is often a structure built, or left unbuilt, on purpose. That structure is called organizational design, and it determines whether a company can adapt when conditions change. What Organizational Design Actually Means Organizational design is not just a chart pinned on a wall. It is the framework that shows how people, roles, and tasks connect to deliver on strategy. It tells you who owns what decision, how information moves, and where accountability sits. What This Looks Like in Practice Consider two examples from the corporate world. A large consumer goods multinational reorganized itself into a handful of core business groups. The result was clearer accountability and faster response to market shifts. Around the same time, a global technology company shifted its focus away from hardware and rebuilt its teams around software and services. Neither company changed its ambition. Both changed how work was organized to support that ambition. A structure built on purpose can carry ambition forward. A structure left unbuilt just carries the same problems into a new shape. Why Most Restructuring Efforts Fail Despite how important this is, most companies get it wrong. Research suggests that a large majority of organizations, well above half, still run on structures that are outdated or unclear. Only a small fraction have models that are genuinely flexible enough to respond to change. This gap explains why so many restructuring efforts fail to deliver what they promised. When leadership changes reporting lines without first fixing the underlying design, the business simply carries its old problems into a new shape. Good organizational design is not about redrawing boxes on a page. It is about reshaping how the company actually works day to day. Picture the chess board again. Every strong opening move protects the pieces that matter most while creating room to grow. A company that gets its design right keeps its core identity intact while improving how decisions are made and how work flows between teams. Why This Matters for African Businesses Businesses across Africa are not exempt from this reality. As companies expand into new states, new countries, or new product lines, the structures that worked at a smaller scale start to strain. Family-run conglomerates transitioning to professional management, banks integrating after a merger, and fast-growing startups scaling their operations all face the same question: does our current structure still serve our strategy? When to Revisit Your Organizational Design There are clear moments when a business needs to revisit its organizational design. Expansion into new markets, mergers and acquisitions, leadership transitions, and sustained performance problems are the most common triggers. In each case, the symptoms show up as confusion over roles, slow decisions, or duplicated effort, but the root cause is almost always structural. Our Eight-Step Organizational Design Model At Traction Outsourcing Limited, we approach this through an eight step model that treats organizational design as a living process rather than a one time event. Assess. We begin by assessing the current state honestly, understanding what is and is not working before changing anything. Strategize. Design choices are aligned to where the business is actually going, not just where it has been. Principles. We set the guiding principles that will shape every structural decision that follows. Structure. The structure itself gets built: reporting lines, groupings, and how work actually flows between teams. Roles. Roles are defined clearly, so ownership and accountability are never ambiguous. Systemize. Systems are put in place to support the new design, rather than leaving it to informal habit. Execute. The new design is executed with discipline, not left half-implemented. Monitor. Results are monitored so the design keeps evolving as the business does. A company does not need a perfect structure. It needs one that matches where the business is going, not where it used to be. Getting this right early saves the cost, confusion, and lost momentum that come from restructuring without a plan. Further Reading: What Is Business Restructuring? , How to Create an Organogram for Your Nigerian Business , Corporate Restructuring . What is organizational design? Organizational design is the framework that shows how people, roles, and tasks connect to deliver on a company's strategy. It defines who owns what decision, how information moves through the business, and where accountability sits. It goes beyond an org chart to shape how work actually happens day to day. Why do most corporate restructuring efforts fail? Most restructuring efforts fail because leadership changes reporting lines or job titles without first fixing the underlying organizational design. Redrawing boxes on a chart does not change how decisions are made or how work flows between teams, so the business ends up carrying its old problems into a new shape. What is Traction Outsourcing's eight-step organizational design model? The model has eight stages: Assess the current state honestly, Strategize by aligning design to business direction, set guiding Principles, build the Structure itself, define Roles clearly, Systemize supporting processes, Execute with discipline, and Monitor results so the design keeps evolving with the business. When should a business revisit its organizational design? The most common triggers are expansion into new markets, mergers and acquisitions, leadership transitions, and sustained performance problems. In each case the visible symptoms, confusion over roles, slow decisions, or duplicated effort, usually point back to a structural cause.

t: A Book That Gets Under Your Skin, in a Good Way
d: What readers are saying about Nigerian Bosses Are Bad, the free e-book by Prince Elijah Abumoye on why Nigerian bosses behave the way they do, and what it would take to change it.
b: A supervisor snaps at a junior staff member in front of the whole office because a report came in late. Everyone in the room goes quiet, eyes down, pretending to work. Nobody says anything. Most people who have worked in Nigeria have either lived this moment or watched it happen to someone else. This is not an unusual scene in Nigerian offices. It happens in Lagos, in Abuja, in Port Harcourt, in small businesses and large ones alike. Nigerian Bosses Are Bad , written by Prince Elijah Abumoye, sits inside these moments and asks a harder question than the title suggests. Not just "why do bosses behave this way," but "what would it take for us to actually change it." The book moves through the foreword and the early chapters with an honesty that can feel uncomfortable before it feels useful. Almost Put It Down, Then Couldn't Stop Reading One reader described exactly that discomfort. Early in the book, before the first chapter properly begins, the tone shifts in a way that almost felt like it was making excuses for bad bosses. The reader admitted to nearly putting the book down at that point, suspicious that it was going soft on behavior that deserved no defense. But reading on changed that impression completely. The book traces bad behavior back to where it actually starts, and makes the case that understanding the root is what allows anything to change. People don't judge intents, they judge actions. It Explains, Without Excusing That distinction sits at the center of the book. A boss who is carrying pressure, fear, or an old wound from years back can come across as harsh or unfair, even when that was never the intention. The same reader noted that almost everyone running a business in Nigeria is carrying some kind of trauma, and that it shapes how they lead, whether they notice it or not. Sometimes it takes an outside voice, or a book like this one, to show a leader something about themselves that they could not see on their own. Not Just What to Do, But Why What stood out most to this reader was that the book "isn't just telling us what to do, but telling us whys and leaving us to make our decisions." That approach makes the book useful for staff and bosses in equal measure. A staff member reading it may finally find language for something they always felt but never explained. A boss reading it with an open mind may recognize themselves in a chapter and choose to lead differently the next day. The Chapter That Stayed With One Reader One chapter in particular stayed with this reader: the story of a social media manager whose work rarely showed up as a clean number on a spreadsheet, and the quiet skill required to explain that value to people who only trust figures. It is a small story, but it captures something bigger about how much of real work in Nigerian offices goes unseen and unmeasured, simply because nobody has learned to talk about it properly. Read It Free Nigerian Bosses Are Bad is available free to read at tolnigeria.com/resources . It was written by Prince Elijah Abumoye, founder of Traction Outsourcing Limited, out of years spent inside Nigerian workplaces, watching good people leave and good leaders struggle to understand why. If you lead a team, it may show you something about yourself. If you work under one, it may finally put words to something you have carried for a while. Either way, it is worth the read. Nigerian Bosses Are Bad is a short e-book by Prince Elijah Abumoye, founder of Traction Outsourcing Limited, about why so many bosses in Nigerian workplaces are seen as unfair or difficult, and what pressure, trauma, and poor structure have to do with it. t: When the CEO Is the Weak Link
d: In many Nigerian companies, the biggest risk to growth is not the economy or the competition. It is the person at the top. Here is how to spot the signs and start turning it around.
b: Every business owner spends hours studying the market, the competition, and the customer. But only a few spend the same hours studying themselves. Yet in many companies across Nigeria today, the biggest risk to growth is not the economy or the competition. It is the person at the top. This is not an easy thing to say to a founder who has poured years into building something from nothing. But it needs saying, because a company can only grow as far as its leader is willing to grow with it. According to the International Labour Organization (ILO), SMEs make up 96 percent of all businesses in Nigeria, provide 84 percent of employment, and contribute 48 percent of the country's GDP. Yet reports cited in the Nigerian press, including a 2022 report from fintech company Kippa, estimate that about 80 percent of businesses in Africa fail within five years of starting. This means that simply surviving that stretch of time already puts a business ahead of most others that started around the same time. Beyond survival, whether the company grows or remains stagnant in one place often comes down to the person running it. Understand How It Starts When you walk into many small and mid-sized businesses, you will notice a pattern of stiff control. The owner still approves every purchase order, no matter how small. Every hire waits for their final nod. Every client email passes through their inbox before it goes out. On the surface, this looks like discipline. In reality, it is a bottleneck wearing the costume of leadership. When a business cannot function for a single day without its owner physically present, that business does not have a strong leader. It has a single point of failure. The same pattern shows up in decision making. Talented staff raise a concern, but once they are ignored more times than they can count, they stop raising it. The business loses the insight and nobody notices. Why Founders Never See It Coming Most founders built their companies by trusting their own instincts and gut feeling, often against advice from people who told them the idea would never work. That instinct served them well early on and gave them the extra kick to make things work against all odds. The trouble starts when the company outgrows what one person can carry, and the founder keeps leading exactly as they did on day one. Success early on can convince a leader that their way is the only way and that everyone must do things in the exact sequence. Some founders have created a culture where junior staff hesitate to challenge them, and the founder can go years without hearing one piece of feedback that would change everything. What This Costs the Business A company led this way pays a quiet but steady price. Skilled employees will leave after getting tired of decisions made without their input. Promising opportunities will stall because they sit on a desk waiting for a signature that takes days to come. Managers will stop managing and start waiting, because they know the real decisions happen elsewhere. A survey carried out by Gallup found that a manager accounts for at least 70 percent of the difference in how engaged employees feel at work. In a founder-led business, also known as a one-man business, the founder is that manager for the whole company. Every hesitation to trust a manager, every ignored suggestion, and every decision pulled back to the top ripples through engagement long before it shows up in a resignation letter. These actions do not affect company growth immediately. They eat the company from the inside out, while the CEO, who was supposedly expected to be the strongest link, watches the rot set in. Issues pile up and show up months later in the form of missed targets nobody can fully explain and staff turnover that keeps repeating for reasons nobody wants to say out loud. How To Stop Being The Weak Link The fix to this founder-led problem does not require you to step back completely or hand over control you are not ready to release. It starts smaller: pick one decision this month that does not need to pass through you, and let a manager own it fully, mistakes included. It also means asking a direct question in meetings and waiting for the answer, rather than waiting for a pause to speak. It does not matter if the response fails to meet your expectation at first. If you sense a gap in their intelligence, get them up to speed with trainings, management books, and/or external consulting to sharpen their minds. The goal is for you, the founder, to gradually become the least intelligent in the room, not by diminishing yourself, but by constantly improving others to their full potential. Over time, staff learn whether their opinions matter by watching what happens after they share one, not by what is written in the handbook. Founders who make this shift often notice something unexpected. The business speeds up when they step back from daily decisions, because the people closest to the work finally have room to do it well. The Real Measure of Leadership A strong CEO builds a team capable of finding answers without them in the room, rather than trying to hold every answer alone. That difference decides whether a business depends on one person or lasts well beyond them. At Traction Outsourcing Limited, we work with founders and leadership teams across Nigeria to build the structures, hiring practices, and management systems that let companies grow past the limits of any single individual, through Business Advisory and Corporate Restructuring engagements built around how your business actually runs. Sometimes the most valuable change we help a business make starts with a conversation the founder did not expect to have about themselves. Book a FREE 30-minute advisory to discuss your needs with us. Further Reading: How to Build a Resilient Management Team , Accountability in Business Nigeria , MD vs CEO in Nigeria , Restructuring Without Losing Your Best People . Sources ThisDay, MSMEs Contribute 48% of Nigeria's GDP, Says ILO (November 2022) BusinessDay, 80% of businesses in Africa fail within five years of establishment: report (July 2022) Gallup, Employees Want a Lot More From Their Managers (2015) How do I know if I am the weak link in my own company? A useful test is whether the business can function for a full day without you physically available. If every purchase, hire, or client email still has to pass through you, or if managers have stopped raising concerns because they have been overruled before, those are signs that decisions are bottlenecking at the top rather than being distributed to the people equipped to make them. What is a single point of failure in a business? A single point of failure is any role or person the business cannot operate without, even briefly. When a founder personally approves every decision, no matter how small, the entire company's output depends on that one person's availability. A resilient business spreads authority so that operations continue smoothly even when any one person, including the founder, is unavailable. How does founder over-involvement affect staff engagement? According to Gallup research, a manager accounts for at least 70 percent of the difference in how engaged their team feels at work. In a founder-led business, the founder is effectively that manager for the whole company. When feedback is ignored and decisions are consistently pulled back to the top, engagement erodes well before it shows up as a resignation, usually appearing first as missed targets and unexplained turnover. How can a founder start delegating without losing control of the business? Start small rather than stepping back all at once. Pick one recurring decision this month that does not need to pass through you, and let a manager own it completely, including the mistakes that come with it. Pair that with genuinely waiting for answers in meetings rather than filling the silence yourself. Staff learn whether their input matters by watching what happens after they give it, not from what is written in a handbook.
