t: Employee Leave and Compensation in Nigeria: A Guide for Employers
d: Annual leave, sick leave, maternity leave, public holidays, and the current minimum wage, explained under the Labour Act.
b: A company in Port Harcourt once lost a National Industrial Court claim over 47 days of untaken annual leave that had quietly built up over six years. The employer's argument, that leave not taken was simply forfeited, had no basis in Nigerian law. That case is a useful reminder that leave and compensation are not soft HR topics, they are compliance obligations with real financial consequences. This guide covers what Nigerian labour law actually requires for annual leave, sick leave, maternity leave, public holidays, and the national minimum wage, and where the law is silent and left to company policy instead. Who the Labour Act Actually Covers The Labour Act (Cap L1, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004) is the primary statute behind most of what follows, but it does not apply to everyone the same way. The Act is written around the term "worker," which in practice covers manual labourers and non-executive clerical staff. Employees exercising administrative, executive, technical, or professional functions sit largely outside the Act's direct provisions and are instead governed mainly by the terms of their employment contract. In practice, most formal employers in Nigeria apply the Act's leave standards, or better, across their entire workforce regardless of this technical distinction, since it is simpler to administer one policy and it avoids the appearance of treating staff unequally. But it is worth knowing the line exists, particularly when a contract is silent on a specific leave type. Annual Leave The statutory minimum is 6 working days of paid annual leave after 12 months of continuous service, rising to 12 working days for young workers under 16, including apprentices. An employee who joins partway through a year does not begin accruing leave until they complete a full 12 months of continuous service. Six days sounds low next to what most Nigerian employees actually receive. In practice, the statutory minimum is treated as a floor, not a target, most formal-sector employers offer 20 to 30 working days a year through the employment contract or internal policy, and that enhanced entitlement is what governs once it is written down. 6 to 30 working days. Statutory minimum is 6 working days after 12 months' service; typical private-sector practice runs 20 to 30 working days a year. Carry-Over and Payout An employer generally cannot pay wages in place of leave the employee has not taken while they remain in service. Leave can be deferred by mutual agreement, but only within limits, the earning and deferral period together must not exceed 24 months. What an employer cannot do is run a blanket "use it or lose it" policy that simply erases unused leave at year end. Where an employee was operationally prevented from taking leave, kept on critical work, denied requests, the leave is not forfeited. If the employment ends before that leave is used, the employer must pay its cash equivalent, calculated at the employee's final salary rate, which is exactly what the Port Harcourt case above turned on. Sick Leave Employees are entitled to up to 12 working days of paid sick leave in a calendar year. To qualify, the illness generally needs to be certified by a registered medical practitioner, informal self-certification is not enough to trigger the statutory entitlement. Sick pay is calculated on normal wages only, excluding overtime and other allowances. Maternity Leave Maternity leave runs to roughly 12 weeks, split before and after childbirth, and applies to female employees. During this period, the Labour Act requires the employer to pay at least 50% of the employee's salary as a statutory floor. A meaningful number of employers pay full salary through the maternity leave period as an enhanced benefit rather than the bare minimum, worth factoring into a competitive policy. An employee may request an extension beyond the standard period for medical reasons affecting her or the baby. Whether that extended period is paid, and at what rate, is left to the employer's discretion and the specifics of the case, there is no blanket statutory answer. Paternity and Other Non-Statutory Leave There is currently no statutory paternity leave requirement for private sector employees in Nigeria. Male federal civil servants are entitled to 14 days of paternity leave following a 2021 Federal Executive Council approval, but that applies to public sector employment specifically. Private employers are free to offer paternity leave as a matter of policy, and a growing number do, but where there is no such policy, male employees typically draw on their annual leave instead. The same applies to study leave, compassionate or bereavement leave, and relief leave, none of these are statutory entitlements under the Act. They exist entirely at the discretion of the employer, through the employment contract, an internal HR policy, or case-by-case approval. Leave Types at a Glance Annual Leave — 6 working days after 12 months' service. Status: Statutory. Sick Leave — Up to 12 working days per year, with medical certification. Status: Statutory. Maternity Leave — ~12 weeks, at least 50% of salary paid. Status: Statutory. Paternity Leave — 14 days (public sector only). Status: Not statutory in private sector. Study, Compassionate, Relief Leave — None. Status: Policy-based only. Public Holidays and Weekly Rest Nigeria observes around 11 public holidays a year, declared as paid work-free days, in addition to annual leave, not counted against it. If a public holiday coincides with a worker's weekly rest day, the worker is not entitled to a substitute day off. Separately, every worker is entitled to at least one weekly rest day of not less than 24 continuous hours after 6 consecutive working days, and that rest day is paid. Where an employee is required to work on a public holiday or their weekly rest day, they are entitled to compensation at the applicable overtime rate, or, alternatively, a corresponding day off within 14 days. Compensation: The National Minimum Wage The national minimum wage in Nigeria is currently ₦70,000 per month, set under the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Act 2024, which raised it from the previous ₦30,000. It applies broadly across the public and private sector, subject to limited statutory exemptions, and non-compliance carries real penalties, including fines and liability for outstanding wage arrears. ₦70,000 / month. Current national minimum wage under the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Act 2024. Beyond the statutory floor, compensation structures in Nigeria vary widely by sector and role, and are shaped as much by market competition for skilled talent as by the law itself. Non-cash benefits matter here too: most competitive employers also offer HMO health coverage alongside salary, since it is one of the benefits Nigerian employees weigh most heavily when comparing job offers. The minimum wage sets the compliance boundary, it does not set a competitive salary. A note on accuracy: Minimum wage figures and leave entitlements are reviewed periodically and can change. This guide reflects the position as understood in July 2026. Confirm current figures against the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment or a qualified HR or legal professional before relying on them for a specific compliance decision. Getting Leave and Compensation Policy Right Most leave disputes in Nigeria do not come from employers deliberately breaking the law. They come from informal policies, an unwritten "use it or lose it" understanding, a verbal promise about paternity leave that was never documented, a payroll system that does not track accrued leave against final pay at exit. None of that shows up as a problem until an employee leaves or a dispute lands in front of the National Industrial Court. How many days of annual leave are employees entitled to in Nigeria? The Labour Act sets a statutory minimum of 6 working days of paid annual leave after 12 months of continuous service, or 12 working days for young workers under 16, including apprentices. In practice, most formal-sector employers in Nigeria offer considerably more, commonly 20 to 30 days a year, through the employment contract or company policy. Is maternity leave paid in Nigeria? Yes, though only partially under the statutory minimum. The Labour Act provides for a maternity leave period of around 12 weeks, split before and after childbirth, during which the employer must pay at least 50% of the employee's salary. Many employers pay full salary through the maternity leave period as an enhanced benefit. How many sick leave days are employees entitled to in Nigeria? Up to 12 working days of paid sick leave in a calendar year, provided the illness is certified by a registered medical practitioner. Sick pay is based on normal wages and does not include overtime or other allowances. What is the current minimum wage in Nigeria? The national minimum wage in Nigeria is 70,000 naira per month, set by the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Act 2024. It applies to employers across the public and private sector, subject to limited exemptions, and is reviewed periodically.

t: How to Register a Company in Nigeria: Complete CAC Registration Guide
d: Business name or limited company, costs, timelines, and what to do after your CAC certificate is issued.
b: If you are asking "how do I start my business in Nigeria," the honest answer starts with one body: the Corporate Affairs Commission. Everything else, tax, banking, contracts, credibility, depends on getting this part right first. An unregistered business can still serve customers and make money, but it cannot open a corporate bank account, cannot bid for most government or corporate contracts, and cannot access loans, grants, or accelerator programmes, nearly all of which ask for proof of registration before they consider an application. Registering with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) under the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020 is what turns a business idea into a legally recognized entity. Business Name or Limited Company? Choosing Your Structure Before you touch the CAC portal, decide what kind of entity you are registering. For most first-time founders, the choice is between two options. Business Name A business name covers sole proprietorships and general partnerships. It has no separate legal personality, which means you, the owner, are personally liable for the business's debts and obligations. It is the cheaper, faster option, and it suits small operations, freelancers, and side businesses that do not yet need the protection or formality of a company structure. Private Limited Company (Ltd) A limited company is a separate legal entity from its owners. Your personal assets are protected from the company's debts, which matters as soon as you are taking on contracts, hiring staff, or raising money. It requires more documentation, a minimum share capital, generally ₦100,000 for a standard private company, and higher compliance obligations going forward, including annual returns. What You Need Before You Start Two or three proposed business names, in order of preference Details of directors, shareholders, and, for a limited company, a company secretary A clear, specific description of your business activities, vague descriptions slow down approval A physical Nigerian address for the business, a P.O. Box is generally not accepted Valid means of identification for everyone involved, scanned in color, black and white scans are a common cause of rejection For a limited company, your proposed share capital and a Memorandum and Articles of Association covering the full scope of the business How to Register with CAC, Step by Step 1. Search and Reserve Your Name Use the CAC public search, available through the CAC portal, to confirm your preferred name is not already taken or too similar to an existing one. Reserve it once confirmed. 2. Complete the Online Application Registration is done through the CAC's online portal. You create an account, fill in the registration form with the details of the owner or directors, and upload your supporting documents. 3. Submit Your Application Complete the registration form on the CAC portal and upload your supporting documents for review. 4. Receive Your Certificate Once your application is approved, your registration certificate is issued digitally, there is no physical document to collect. A business name is typically ready within a few business days. A limited company generally takes longer, often one to two weeks, depending on how complete and accurate your documents are. After Registration: Tax and What Comes Next Your CAC certificate is the starting point, not the finish line. A registered business still needs a Tax Identification Number (TIN) to open a corporate bank account and to remain compliant. There has been discussion of eventually merging the CAC registration number with a business's TIN so the two are issued together, but as things currently stand, TIN registration is still its own separate step handled through the relevant tax authority, not something that happens automatically the moment your CAC certificate is issued. Budget the time for it as a distinct task until that changes. Beyond tax registration, most growing businesses also need a VAT certificate if applicable to their activities, a corporate bank account (which requires your RC number and TIN), and, if the brand name itself is valuable, a trademark filed in the appropriate class, which is a separate process from CAC registration entirely. None of this is optional if you intend to operate formally, open institutional doors, or eventually raise money. Common Mistakes That Get Applications Rejected Submitting black and white identification scans instead of color Proposing a name too similar to one already registered Writing vague objects of association instead of a specific description of what the business actually does Using a P.O. Box instead of a physical address Incomplete director or shareholder information on a limited company application Each of these is a minor detail on its own, but any one of them can send an application back for correction, adding days or weeks to a process that should take days. Registering a Business in Nigeria as a Foreigner or From the Diaspora Living outside Nigeria does not, by itself, change how you register a business. The CAC portal is online, and a Nigerian citizen abroad registering a wholly Nigerian-owned company follows the exact same process, and faces the exact same requirements, as someone registering from Lagos or Abuja. What actually changes the process is ownership, not location. A business is treated as having foreign participation the moment any non-Nigerian individual or foreign entity holds shares in it, even a small percentage. Once that is the case, the company must also register with the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission (NIPC), obtain a Business Permit from the Federal Ministry of Interior, and meet a minimum share capital requirement that is significantly higher than what a wholly Nigerian-owned company needs to declare. If the business intends to bring in foreign staff, Expatriate Quota approval is a further step. These thresholds are reviewed periodically, so confirm the current requirements with NIPC or a professional before you structure the shareholding, rather than relying on a figure from an older article. A wholly Nigerian-owned company, regardless of where its owner lives, does not trigger any of this. If you are a Nigerian in the diaspora registering a business you will own outright, you can go through the standard CAC process described above. Should You Register Yourself or Use a Professional? The CAC portal is built for self-service, and plenty of founders register their own business name without issue. Where it gets more complicated is everything the registration certificate does not cover on its own: choosing the right structure for where the business is actually going, getting the objects of association specific enough to hold up, sorting out TIN and VAT registration, and building the internal structure, job descriptions, and reporting lines a business needs the moment it hires its first employee. That is the gap Traction Outsourcing works in. Registration is the first phase of our startup structuring service , which covers CAC registration, your TIN, VAT certificate, trademark filing, and your official CAMA-compliant communication letters, then continues into building the organogram, job descriptions, and policies your business needs to actually run once it exists on paper. If you want to see what that structure actually looks like, read how to create an organogram for your Nigerian business next. How do I start my business in Nigeria? Start by choosing a business structure, either a business name or a limited liability company, then register it with the Corporate Affairs Commission. Once registered, move on to tax registration, opening a corporate bank account, and building the internal structure your business needs to actually run. How do I register a company in Nigeria? You register with the Corporate Affairs Commission, either yourself through the CAC portal or through an accredited agent. The process involves reserving a name, preparing your documents, submitting your application, then receiving your certificate. What is the difference between a business name and a limited company in Nigeria? A business name has no separate legal personality, so the owner is personally liable for its debts. A limited company is a separate legal entity, which limits personal liability, but comes with more documentation and higher ongoing compliance obligations. Can Nigerians living abroad register a company in Nigeria? Yes. A Nigerian citizen abroad registering a wholly Nigerian-owned company follows the same CAC process as anyone registering from within Nigeria, since the portal is fully online. Location does not change the requirements, ownership does.

t: Tall Poppy Syndrome: Why Your Closest Friends Are Often the Last to Become Your Customers
d: Friends like your posts and still buy elsewhere. Here is what Tall Poppy Syndrome reveals about growth, friendship, and where your real customers come from.
b: Your friends know exactly what you do. They came to the launch, liked the posts, then bought the exact same thing from someone else. If that has happened to you, it is rarely as personal as it feels. It has a name, and it is older than you think. An Old Instinct With a New Name Tall Poppy Syndrome was named in Australia and New Zealand in the 1980s, but the instinct predates the phrase by two thousand years. The Roman historian Livy recorded the source of the name: King Tarquinius Superbus, asked by his son how to control a rival city, said nothing. He simply walked into his garden and knocked the heads off the tallest poppies. Japan has its own version, the nail that sticks up gets hammered down. Chile calls it chaquetear, to pull someone back by the jacket. People rarely resent your growth because they dislike you. They resent it because it measures the distance between where you have gone and where you both expected to stay. What the Research Shows In 2018, Women of Influence surveyed 1,501 people across Canadian workplaces. Nearly nine in ten said their achievements had been undermined at work, and about half named their own friends as the source. A 2023 follow-up surveyed 4,710 women across 103 countries and found 86.8 percent had experienced the same pattern. Undermining someone privately and simply choosing not to pay them for their work are the same instinct, expressed differently. Choosing not to buy from a friend's business rarely feels like jealousy from the inside. It feels like loyalty to an old version of the relationship, one where nobody had to pay anybody for anything. Why Friends Pull Back Most friendships form between people close in circumstance and stage of life. That closeness is the floor the friendship stands on. When one person starts visibly rising, the floor tilts. Access that used to be free now has a price attached, and paying you can feel like renegotiating a friendship rather than simply buying a service. Nobody frames it as jealousy to themselves, but not buying quietly protects the old equality all the same. Grace, Not Grudges Not every friend who never became a customer is cutting you down. Some cannot afford what you offer, some do not need it, others are loyal to a provider they already trust. What is worth naming is different: the friend who dismisses your work to others or spends money elsewhere just to make a point. That is Tall Poppy Syndrome in its sharper form. What This Means for Your Business None of this means shrinking to stay comfortable for people. It means being realistic about where your early revenue comes from. Friends who knew you before you built anything are often the last to buy, because buying from you means mentally reclassifying you from friend to service provider. Your first real customers are more likely to be strangers who meet you as a business owner from day one, with no old relationship to renegotiate. That is where structure earns its keep. A stranger has no history with you to fall back on, so what convinces them is what they can see: clear process, a professional handbook, a team that knows its roles. Startup structuring builds exactly that foundation. Business advisory support helps founders further along see the gaps a friend's goodwill used to paper over, and staff outsourcing puts the right people in place to carry it. Traction Outsourcing Limited works with growing Nigerian businesses on exactly this. What is Tall Poppy Syndrome in business? Tall Poppy Syndrome is the social instinct to resent or pull back from someone who visibly outgrows their peer group. In business, it often shows up as friends and early acquaintances becoming quieter supporters, not louder ones, once a founder's business starts to succeed. Why do friends struggle to support a growing business? Friendship is usually built on relative equality. When one person visibly grows through a business, a promotion, or new opportunities, that balance shifts. It is rarely malice. More often it is discomfort with a relationship that no longer feels level, and that discomfort quietly shows up as friends going elsewhere for what you sell. Should a founder stop growing to avoid Tall Poppy Syndrome? No. The answer is not to shrink to keep people comfortable. It is to understand where your early customers will realistically come from, usually people who meet you as a business owner first, and to build the structure that lets strangers trust you quickly since your oldest friends may take longer.

t: Why Nigerian Startups Fail Within Their First Five Years
d: More than nine in ten Nigerian SMEs fail within five years. A structural diagnosis of why, and what separates the ones that survive.
b: Every Nigerian founder has sat across from a business that was, on paper, supposed to work. A good product. A real market. A founder willing to work harder than almost anyone around them. And still, within a few years, the business quietly stopped opening its doors. Nobody wrote a press release. There was no dramatic collapse, just a slow decline in orders, a landlord who stopped getting paid on time, and eventually, silence. This is not a story about a lack of ambition. Nigeria has no shortage of ambition. It is a story about structure, and the absence of it. The Scale of the Problem The numbers here are difficult to look away from. Data from the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria and the National Bureau of Statistics shows that more than nine in ten Nigerian SMEs fail within their first five years of operation. A separate analysis tracking Nigerian startups between 2010 and 2018 put the failure rate at just over sixty percent, the highest among Africa's major business ecosystems during that period. 9 in 10 Nigerian SMEs fail within their first five years (SMEDAN/NBS) 60% Nigerian startup failure rate 2010-2018, highest in Africa's major ecosystems 4 in 10 Startup failures globally caused by building something nobody needed (CB Insights) These are not businesses that failed because Nigeria lacks customers, capital, or talent. Nigeria has all three, unevenly distributed, but present. What consistently emerges from research into these failures is a narrower, more specific set of causes: poor marketing strategy, an inability to correctly identify the paying customer, the absence of a real business plan, wrong location decisions, and what researchers plainly call managerial deficiency. None of these are about the product. All of them are about structure. The Global Pattern, Localised This is not uniquely a Nigerian problem, but Nigeria's version of it is sharper. Global research from CB Insights found that the single largest cause of startup failure worldwide is building something the market never actually needed, a pattern responsible for roughly four in ten failures. In Nigeria, that same failure mode is amplified by higher logistics costs, currency volatility, and thinner margins for error. A business in a more forgiving market can survive a few months of miscalculated demand. A Nigerian business operating on tight margins, with naira-denominated revenue and often dollar-denominated costs, frequently cannot. Several well-funded Nigerian startups have shut down or significantly scaled back in recent years after discovering, sometimes tens of millions of dollars into operation, that their cost per transaction exceeded what customers were willing to pay. The lesson from these cases is rarely about the idea. It is almost always about the absence of a structure rigorous enough to catch the problem before the money ran out. A good idea is never the scarce resource in Nigeria. The scarce resource is the structure that lets a good idea become a sustainable business. Structure Is Not Bureaucracy There is a persistent myth among early-stage Nigerian founders that structure is something you add once you have made it, a layer of formality reserved for companies large enough to need policies and processes. This gets the sequence backwards. The businesses that survive long enough to need that formality are, almost without exception, the ones that built basic structural discipline in from the beginning. Structure, at the early stage, is not an organogram or a thick policy manual. It is a small number of unglamorous decisions made deliberately instead of by accident: A real understanding of who the paying customer is and what they can actually afford A cost structure that has been tested against realistic sales volumes rather than optimistic ones Clear ownership of who is responsible for which decisions A cash flow discipline that separates what the business owns from what the founder is personally funding Employment and governance documentation, including a proper employee handbook and role definitions, that means the business can function if a key person leaves Businesses that skip this stage tend to discover their structural gaps at the worst possible moment, usually when a cash shortfall, a key staff departure, or a sudden spike in demand exposes exactly how much of the operation was being held together informally. This is also where Corporate Restructuring becomes relevant for businesses that have already been operating for years but have never addressed the structural gaps that have been quietly accumulating. What Separates the Businesses That Survive The Nigerian businesses that make it past the five-year mark share a pattern that has little to do with luck. They price based on what their actual customer can pay, not what a customer in a more affluent market might pay. They build governance and financial discipline while still small, when the cost of fixing a mistake is a difficult conversation rather than a bankruptcy filing. They separate personal and business finances early, so a bad month does not become an existential threat. And critically, they bring in outside advisory perspective before problems become visible, not after. That last point is the one founders resist most, often for understandable reasons. Asking for structured guidance can feel like admitting the plan was incomplete. In practice, the founders who engage Business Advisory support earliest are consistently the ones who avoid the failure patterns that show up so reliably in the data. Building the Structure Before You Need It Traction Outsourcing Limited works with Nigerian founders and growing businesses on exactly this problem. Our Startup Structuring service builds the operational, financial, and organisational foundations that keep a good idea from becoming another statistic. This includes business development planning, financial and operational framework design, HR and people systems, and the governance documentation that lets a business survive its own early mistakes. For businesses already past the early stage but carrying structural gaps accumulated over years, our Business Advisory service provides the outside perspective and the structured intervention that internal teams are rarely positioned to deliver on their own. And where the gap is in people and staffing, Staff Outsourcing and HR Management provides the employment infrastructure without the overhead of building an internal HR function from scratch. Why do Nigerian startups fail? Most Nigerian startup failures trace back to structural gaps rather than a single dramatic mistake. The absence of clear roles, reporting lines, documented processes, and financial discipline lets problems accumulate until a cash shortfall, a key staff departure, or a sudden spike in demand exposes how much of the operation was held together informally. What percentage of Nigerian startups fail within five years? Data from SMEDAN and the National Bureau of Statistics shows that more than nine in ten Nigerian SMEs fail within their first five years of operation. A separate analysis of Nigerian startups between 2010 and 2018 put the failure rate at over sixty percent, the highest among Africa's major business ecosystems during that period. How can I prevent my Nigerian startup from failing? Build the organisational structure, reporting lines, and documentation before the business needs them under pressure. This means a clear understanding of who the paying customer is, a cost structure tested against realistic sales volumes, defined roles and decision rights, and cash flow discipline from the start. Structure is not bureaucracy. It is what lets a business survive its own growth. What is startup structuring in Nigeria? t: How to Create an Organogram for Your Nigerian Business
d: A step-by-step guide to mapping reporting lines and structure, with a worked example for a real estate company.
b: Designing a corporate organogram is not just about drawing lines on a piece of paper. It is about mapping the nervous system of your business. In our work at Traction Outsourcing Limited, we often see businesses that function like a series of busy hallways where everyone runs into everyone else, but nobody knows who owns the final outcome. A clear organogram solves this by turning chaos into intentional order. When your team members know exactly where they fit and who they answer to, you stop paying for overlapping roles and start paying for clear results. Step 1: Audit Your Operational Reality Do not start by drawing a dream team that you hope to hire next year. Start by writing down every task your business completes today. Who manages the daily finances? Who handles client communication? Who makes the final decision when a project stalls? Map the functions that currently exist. If you find that one person is doing the work of three departments, that is your first insight. An organogram must reflect the actual flow of work, not just the desired aesthetic. Step 2: Group Functions by Impact Once you have your list of tasks, group them into core departments. Most growing businesses in Nigeria thrive when they separate these four pillars: Operations: The people who build, maintain, or deliver the core product or service. Finance & Administration: The gatekeepers of the budget, legal compliance, and internal office stability. Growth & Sales: The engine responsible for new revenue and client relationships. Talent & Culture: The team that ensures the right people are in the right seats and that the workplace remains a place where people want to stay. Step 3: Define Reporting Lines and Authority This is where most structures fail. You must decide if your culture is top-down or collaborative. For a small business, a flat structure might work. As you scale, you need vertical accountability. Every person must have one clear supervisor. If an employee reports to two managers, you have created a bottleneck where decisions go to die. Step 4: Keep It Scalable Build your organogram to be modular. If you are a startup, you might have one person acting as both the Sales Lead and the Customer Support Manager. That is fine. Just ensure the organogram shows these as two distinct functional boxes even if one person occupies both. This way, when the time comes to hire, you simply slice the role in half and bring on a new person to take over the support function. Consider This Example: A Real Estate Company Imagine you work with a young real estate management firm. You might organize it this way: the Director sits at the top, and underneath, three primary leads carry the business. Sample Organogram for a Real Estate Management Firm Operations Lead Property maintenance, listings, site inspections, vendor negotiations, contractor relations Sales & Brokerage Lead Property listings, client tours, partnerships & communication, contract agreements Finance & Admin Lead Rent collection, disbursement protocols, cost & expenditure management, legal paperwork If you are just starting, you might be all three leads. You draw the boxes for all three, but you write your own name in each. As the business grows, you hire a person for each box. The structure stays the same, but the burden on your personal capacity decreases. Your organogram is a living document. If your business is failing to hit its targets, the answer is often found in the lines you drew between the boxes. Review It Like You Mean It Review your organogram from time to time, usually every six months or annually. Remove the friction, clarify the reporting, and give your people the space to execute their roles and achieve their targets with brutal execution. This Is a Functional Organogram What has been described above is known as a functional organogram . There are three other types, hierarchical, flat, and matrix, however every business between zero and three years old should focus on the functional organogram. During this stage of your company's growth, you want to improve employee effectiveness at work, efficiency at handling tasks, and job satisfaction. You want to lay less emphasis on who wields what authority and more on who gets what done. If you have not yet registered the business itself, start there first. Read our guide on how to register a company in Nigeria before you build the organogram, the structure works best once the entity behind it legally exists. What type of organogram should a new business use? A functional organogram, which is the structure described in this guide. There are three other types, hierarchical, flat, and matrix, but businesses between zero and three years old should focus on the functional structure, since the priority at that stage is employee effectiveness, efficiency, and clarity over who gets things done, not who holds the most authority. How do I create an organogram for a real estate company? Start with the director at the top, then split the business into its core functions. For a young real estate management firm, that usually means an Operations Lead handling property maintenance, listings, and vendor relations; a Sales and Brokerage Lead handling client tours, partnerships, and contract agreements; and a Finance and Admin Lead handling rent collection, disbursement, and legal paperwork. If you are a solo founder, you can occupy all three boxes yourself and hire into each one as the business grows. How do I create an organogram in Nigeria? Audit the tasks your business actually performs today, group them into core departments such as Operations, Finance and Administration, Growth and Sales, and Talent and Culture, give every person one clear supervisor, and design the structure to stay modular as you hire. Traction Outsourcing Limited helps Nigerian businesses build and review this kind of structure directly. I need help creating an organogram. Where do I start? Start by listing every task your business completes today rather than the roles you eventually want. The gaps and overlaps in that list point directly to how your organogram should be structured. If you would rather have this done for you, Traction Outsourcing Limited offers business advisory and structuring support for Nigerian SMEs.

t: How to Write an Employee Handbook for a Nigerian SME
d: Most Nigerian SMEs run on memory instead of policy. Here is why a handbook is one of the highest-leverage documents a growing business can build.
b: A client once called us in the middle of a crisis that had nothing to do with sales, cash flow, or competition. Two staff members had gotten into a dispute in front of customers. One had missed work repeatedly without explanation. The business owner wanted to know what she could do about it. When we asked what her disciplinary policy said about repeated absenteeism, there was a long pause. There was no policy. There had never been one. Every decision about conduct, leave, and discipline had been made in the moment, based on mood, memory, and whichever version of fairness felt right that day. This is not a rare situation. It is the default condition of most growing Nigerian businesses. Why This Keeps Happening Academic research into HR practices among Nigerian SMEs consistently points to the same pattern: human resource decisions are rarely handled by a dedicated function. In the large majority of small and medium businesses, HR decisions rest entirely with the owner or managing director, made informally and reactively rather than through any documented framework. There is nothing unusual about this. Most businesses start as one person doing everything, and structure tends to arrive only after growth has already made the absence of structure painful. The cost of that delay shows up in ways owners do not always connect back to the missing policy. Recent workforce data shows that a majority of Nigerian employers report real difficulty finding candidates whose expectations, skills, and conduct match what the business actually needs. Some of that mismatch is about skill. A significant part of it is about expectations that were never written down in the first place, so no one, including the employer, was ever entirely sure what "meeting expectations" meant. What a Handbook Actually Does An employee handbook is not a formality for businesses that have "made it." It is a governance tool, and it does three specific jobs that nothing else in a small business does as efficiently. It removes ambiguity before conflict arrives. Disputes over lateness, leave, dress code, or termination almost always escalate faster when there is no written standard to point to. A handbook converts what would otherwise be a personal disagreement between an owner and a staff member into a question of whether documented policy was followed. That shift alone defuses a large share of workplace conflict before it starts. It protects the business legally. Nigerian labour law gives employers real obligations around termination notice, working hours, and conditions of service. A business without a handbook is not exempt from those obligations; it is simply operating without evidence that it has communicated them. When a dispute reaches a labour office or a court, the absence of a documented policy tends to be read against the employer, regardless of how reasonable the underlying decision actually was. It sets the culture before the culture sets itself. Every business has a culture, whether or not anyone designed it. Left undocumented, culture tends to be shaped by whoever is loudest, whoever has been there longest, or whoever the owner likes best. A handbook lets you decide, in advance and in writing, what kind of workplace you are actually building. What Belongs in a Nigerian SME Handbook A functional handbook for a growing Nigerian business does not need to be a two-hundred-page corporate manual. It needs to be complete enough to answer the questions that come up most often, and specific enough that no one has to guess. At minimum, it should cover: working hours and attendance expectations, leave entitlements including annual, sick, and maternity or paternity leave, a clear code of conduct, a disciplinary procedure with defined steps rather than vague language, grounds and process for termination, confidentiality obligations, and a grievance channel that lets staff raise concerns without fear of retaliation. Each of these should be written in plain language that a new hire can read once and actually understand, not legal phrasing borrowed from a template with no relevance to how the business actually runs. The Real Cost of Skipping This Step Business owners often delay writing a handbook because it feels like a task for later, once the company is "big enough" to need one. In practice, the businesses that suffer most from the absence of a handbook are the ones still small enough that one bad hire, one mishandled dispute, or one inconsistent decision can meaningfully damage morale across the entire team. A ten-person company has far less room to absorb the fallout of an unclear termination than a two-hundred-person one does. The smaller the business, the higher the relative cost of getting people decisions wrong, and the more a handbook actually matters. Building It Properly A handbook that is copied from the internet and never adapted to your actual business is close to useless. It needs to reflect your real working hours, your real leave structure, your real disciplinary process, and Nigerian labour law as it applies to your specific sector and state. Getting this right the first time saves you from having to rebuild it later, usually in the middle of a dispute, which is the worst possible time to be writing policy. Traction Outsourcing has built handbooks, codes of conduct, and full HR policy frameworks for businesses across manufacturing, hospitality, real estate, and professional services in Nigeria. We know what belongs in yours, and what does not. Why does a Nigerian SME need an employee handbook? Without a written handbook, policy exists only in the founder's memory, applied inconsistently and impossible to enforce fairly. A handbook turns informal understanding into a document every employee can be held to equally. What should be included in a Nigerian employee handbook? A working handbook covers company policy, conduct expectations, leave and attendance rules, disciplinary procedure, and the practical day-to-day questions new employees actually ask, not just a legal boilerplate. What happens if a business skips having an employee handbook? Disputes get settled inconsistently, expectations vary by manager, and the business has no documented standard to point to when a disagreement over conduct or policy ends up in front of a court or tribunal.

t: The Dangers of Proximity to Success
d: Access without preparation is a trap dressed up as opportunity. A true story about what happens when proximity replaces a real financial foundation.
b: A couple of years ago, one hot afternoon, I met Rita in Abuja. She ran a small restaurant in a village in Kurudu. At that time, I was working on a project on one of our sites and I had not had breakfast. When I ordered, I was not expecting much from the makeshift restaurant shed that could barely fit seven people. As a result, I was surprised that her food was great, the surroundings were clean, and notably, her English was superb. I struck up a conversation with her about how good her food was, and she went on to tell me about how she was a chef. One thing led to another, and we found ourselves talking about the restaurants she visited in Germany, Australia, the UK, and so many other countries. I was curious, of course, how you could visit all the dream countries of an average Nigerian and still be selling tantalizing Jollof rice in a makeshift shed in a village. Rita explained that she worked with a boss who gave her access. Within three months of working with him, she got her passport and could travel with him locally on private jets and internationally on commercial airlines. Within a year, she found herself spending all her salary and allowances trying to meet up with the image and standard of those she found around her. When he finally had to leave Nigeria, she struggled to maintain the lifestyle. She struggled to fit in with her own people, the same people she had before she got the job. When she started a restaurant immediately after, she targeted the same people in her boss's financial and social class. They never came. She burned through her savings and had to face reality. That reality is her current restaurant in Kurudu village. Her story helped me understand a vital truth about unmetered proximity to success: access, without preparation, is a trap dressed up as an opportunity. When Proximity Becomes a Distortion If you look closely around our professional circles, you will realize Rita is not an isolated case. Her story is a quiet pattern playing out all the time. There is a well-documented psychological principle behind what happened to her. Social Comparison Theory, which dates back to the 1950s, argues that when we do not have a clear baseline for who we are, we simply borrow the identity of whoever is closest to us. Upward social comparison, measuring yourself against someone doing better, can either inspire or damage you, depending on whether you genuinely believe their level of success is within your reach. For Rita, the comparison was not gradual. It was total immersion. She was not just observing success from a distance; she was sitting inside it, traveling inside it, and eating inside it every single day. Without a baseline framework for how that world actually operated, her mind did the only thing it could do: it started treating that borrowed world as her own. This is where the danger begins. Proximity without context does not teach you how successful people think. It teaches you how they spend. We see it all the time with lifestyle inflation. It is that subtle shift where luxuries slowly start feeling like basic necessities. For Rita, the process was even more insidious because the income was not even hers. She was consuming a lifestyle funded by someone else's wealth, in someone else's name, on someone else's timeline. And when that person left, the lifestyle did not leave quietly. It left a void she felt compelled to fill. Lifestyle creep is incredibly common among young adults who experience a sudden jump in access or income. What makes it dangerous for many Nigerians who find themselves in similar positions is that the spending is not driven by an actual increase in earnings. It is driven purely by an increase in exposure. There is a massive gulf between the two. The Numbers Behind the Pattern Rita's story might feel deeply personal, but the data confirms it is structural. Data on Nigerian SMEs shows an overwhelming majority fold within the first five years, mirroring global trends where nearly half of business failures happen simply because there is no real market demand for what they are selling. This is rarely a story about bad products. It is a story about targeting the wrong people. When Rita opened her restaurant, she knew how to cook. Her food was genuinely good. What she did not know was her customer. She had spent so much time in the orbit of wealth that she had lost the ability to accurately see the market she actually belonged to. She aimed her pricing, her aesthetic, and her expectations at a clientele that had no particular reason to drive to Kurudu for a meal. Many Nigerian businesses collapse not because of a lack of skill or effort, but because of miscalibrated expectations and a fundamental misunderstanding of who their customers are and how much those customers are actually willing to spend. This is the second danger of unmetered proximity to success. It does not just distort your personal spending; it distorts your professional judgment. It recalibrates your entire sense of what is normal, what is achievable, and who you are building for. What Rita's Story Tells Us About Our Careers These lessons apply whether you are a student, a climbing professional, or an entrepreneur trying to scale. Access is not the same as preparation. Being close to success is not the same as being ready for it. Rita had access to business-class travel, fine dining, and high-level conversations, but none of that translated into capital, systems, or business knowledge when she needed it. Proximity gave her exposure, not a foundation. Your environment shapes your baseline without your permission. When the people around you set a lavish standard, your brain quietly adopts that standard as the bare minimum. You stop seeing it as exceptional and start seeing it as normal. This happens gradually to everyone. The only question is whether you are self-aware enough to notice it happening before making irreversible financial decisions. Knowing your actual market is a strategy, not a compromise. Rita's restaurant in Kurudu is not a failure of ambition; it is a failure of targeting. There is a thriving market in Kurudu, and she is successfully serving it today. The tragedy is not where she ended up. The tragedy is that she spent her life savings chasing a customer who was never coming, when the customers who would genuinely value her work were right in front of her. Knowing your market is the single most important strategic decision you can make. The Advisory Gap Nobody Talks About What Rita needed, and what many people in her situation need, was not more access. It was structured guidance. She needed someone to sit with her before she opened that restaurant and ask the uncomfortable questions: Who is your customer? What can they afford? What are you building toward, and what do you actually have right now to build with? That kind of raw, grounded conversation is rare. Most people navigate their careers and businesses based entirely on what they see around them, what their oga is doing, what their colleagues are spending, and what their peers seem to have. Very few people have access to honest, structured advisory support that helps them separate where they are from where they are going, and build a realistic bridge between the two. This is exactly the work we do at Traction Outsourcing. Alongside a team of experienced professionals, we offer career and business advisory services designed to help individuals and organizations build from a place of clarity rather than comparison. Whether you are a young professional trying to figure out your next move, an entrepreneur preparing to launch, or someone who has found themselves caught in a reality shift and needs a hard reset, the conversation starts by understanding your actual reality, not the one you have been borrowing. Rita's food is still good. It was always good. What changed the outcome of her story was not her skill; it was the absence of a plan rooted in truth. You do not have to make that same mistake. What are the dangers of proximity to success? Being close to successful people or opportunities can create the illusion of readiness without the substance behind it, access is mistaken for preparation, and the gap only becomes visible once real pressure tests it. Why does access without preparation often fail? Opportunity without a real financial or business foundation underneath it tends to collapse under its own weight, since proximity can open a door but cannot substitute for the capability needed to walk through it.

t: The Real Cost of a Bad Hire in Nigeria (And How to Avoid It)
d: A bad hire costs far more than a salary. What the data says about the true cost of hiring wrong, and how structured recruitment prevents it.
b: A growing Abuja business needs an operations manager urgently. The founder is stretched thin, interviews are rushed, and a confident candidate with an impressive CV gets the offer within a week. Four months later, projects are behind schedule, two junior staff have quietly resigned, and the founder is back where they started, except now with a severance package to pay, a damaged team, and the same vacant role still open. This pattern repeats across Nigerian businesses more often than most owners admit. The cost of a bad hire rarely announces itself. It shows up slowly, in missed deadlines and quiet resignations, long after the decision that caused it. What the Data Actually Says The most widely cited benchmark comes from the United States Department of Labor, which estimates that a bad hire costs a business a minimum of thirty percent of that employee's first-year salary, purely in direct replacement costs. That figure is described as conservative for a reason. The Society for Human Resource Management puts the fuller cost, once lost productivity and management time are included, between fifty and two hundred percent of annual salary depending on seniority, with executive-level bad hires sitting at the top of that range. 30% Minimum direct replacement cost as a share of the employee's first-year salary (US DoL) 200% Upper end of total cost including lost productivity and management time for senior roles (SHRM) 3 in 4 Employers who admit to having hired the wrong person for a role at some point (CareerBuilder) These figures were built around Western labour markets, but the underlying mechanics translate directly to Nigeria, often with the damage compounding faster. A Nigerian business rehiring for the same role a second time within a year is not just repeating a recruitment fee. It is absorbing the cost of statutory notice or severance, the delay in productivity while the seat sits empty again, and the reputational cost among remaining staff who watched the first hire fail. There is a local dimension that pure salary multipliers do not capture. Recent workforce research shows that a majority of Nigerian employers report genuine difficulty finding candidates who match what the role actually requires. That skills mismatch pushes businesses toward rushed hiring simply to fill a seat. And rushed hiring is precisely the condition under which bad hires happen. The salary paid to a bad hire is the smallest part of the loss. The larger damage comes from three places that rarely appear on a balance sheet. Where the Damage Actually Comes From Management time. A manager or founder dealing with an underperforming hire spends a disproportionate share of their week correcting mistakes, having difficult conversations, and redoing work that should not need redoing. That is time not spent on growth, on clients, or on the parts of the business that actually generate revenue. Team morale. A bad hire who is allowed to stay too long sends a quiet signal to the rest of the team about what the business is willing to tolerate. Strong performers notice when weak performance goes unaddressed, and some of them start looking elsewhere. This connects directly to the accountability culture the business has built, or failed to build. The second hiring cycle. Every bad hire that fails means the business is effectively paying for the same vacancy twice: once for the person who did not work out, and again for the replacement search. If the replacement search is conducted the same way as the first, the outcome is likely to be the same. Why Structured Recruitment Prevents This Most bad hires are not the result of bad luck. They are the result of a hiring process that relied too heavily on a strong interview performance and too little on structured evaluation. Research on hiring methodology consistently shows that structured interviews, where every candidate is assessed against the same defined criteria, predict job performance far more reliably than open-ended conversation. The businesses that avoid repeat bad hires tend to share the same discipline: They define the role and its success metrics in detail before the search begins, not during it They run every candidate through the same structured process instead of relying on gut feeling They verify claims through reference and background checks rather than taking a CV at face value Where the role is critical, they use an experienced recruitment partner who has the vetting infrastructure and the distance to evaluate objectively This is exactly what ATH Recruiters , a brand of Traction Outsourcing Limited, is built to do. Our structured vetting process screens candidates against the role before they reach your interview, not after. We handle sourcing, screening, and verification so the shortlist you receive has already been tested against your requirements, not just their own CV. For businesses that need more than recruitment, our Staff Outsourcing and HR Management service covers the full employment lifecycle, from onboarding through performance management, so the hire that passes the recruitment process is also set up to succeed in the role. And if the pattern of bad hires is a symptom of a deeper organisational problem, such as vague roles, unclear reporting lines, or no performance management structure, our Business Advisory service addresses the root cause. How much does a bad hire cost a company in Nigeria? A bad hire costs significantly more than the salary paid. Direct replacement costs alone are estimated at a minimum of 30% of the employee's first-year salary, with the fuller cost including lost productivity, management time, and team disruption running between 50% and 200% of annual salary depending on seniority. In Nigeria, the damage often compounds faster because of re-advertising costs, re-onboarding time, and the morale impact on the team that watched the first hire fail. What causes a bad hire in Nigeria? Bad hires most often come from rushed, informal recruitment: vague job descriptions, no structured interview process, and no clear definition of what success in the role looks like before the search begins. Skills mismatch is also a significant factor in the Nigerian market, where employers report genuine difficulty finding candidates who match role requirements, which pushes businesses toward filling the seat quickly rather than correctly. How does structured recruitment prevent bad hires? Structured recruitment prevents bad hires by defining the role and its success metrics before the search begins, running every candidate through the same evaluation criteria, verifying claims through reference and background checks, and using experienced recruitment partners who assess candidates objectively without the time pressure that leads to rushed decisions. b: Company Updates Traction Outsourcing Launches 24/7 Virtual Client Support Traction Outsourcing Limited has launched a 24-hour online client support programme, giving clients a direct digital line to the firm at any hour of the day, regardless of their time zone. By Traction Outsourcing Limited · July 2026 Starting this month, clients of Traction Outsourcing will no longer have to work around a 9-to-5 window to reach the firm online. Whether a client is raising a concern late at night, following up from a different time zone, or simply cannot get through during regular business hours, the new programme ensures someone is always available to respond digitally. The service covers all core touchpoints, HR advisory, recruitment, business solutions, and general client enquiries, through a dedicated online support desk built to run around the clock. The programme covers digital channels only and does not extend to in-person, walk-in support at the office. Why This Matters for Clients Traction Outsourcing works with businesses across Nigeria and increasingly with partners outside the country. A client in a different time zone should not have to wait half a day just to get a response to a simple question. The 24-hour programme closes that gap. It means faster resolution on urgent HR matters, quicker turnaround on recruitment enquiries, and a support system that keeps pace with clients rather than making them wait on it. A BPO and HR Partner Firm for Multinationals in Nigeria For multinationals operating in Nigeria, and for international businesses evaluating a business process outsourcing partner before entering the market, availability outside Lagos or Abuja business hours often decides whether an issue gets resolved quickly or sits for a day. Traction Outsourcing works as a BPO and HR partner firm covering staff outsourcing and HR management, executive and general recruitment through ATH Recruiters, employee training, business advisory, and corporate restructuring. The 24/7 virtual client support desk extends that relationship beyond standard working hours, so a multinational coordinating from a different time zone, or a business development team following up outside the typical 9-to-5, still gets a direct response from a real support desk rather than an out-of-office message. How It Works Clients can reach the support desk online through WhatsApp or email, with every enquiry logged and tracked from first contact to resolution. A dedicated team monitors these channels in shifts, so a query raised at 2am gets the same attention as one raised at 2pm. Where an issue requires escalation to a specialist or account manager, the support desk manages that handoff internally, so clients are not left repeating themselves to different people. Prince Elijah Abumoye, founder of Traction Outsourcing Limited, said: "Business does not stop when the office closes. Our clients have needs that come up outside standard working hours, and increasingly, our clients are not even in the same time zone as us. This programme is about meeting them where they are, when they need us, not when it is convenient for us." Getting Support Clients can now reach Traction Outsourcing at any time through direct calls on 0707 870 7777, WhatsApp at 0805 203 3145, or by email at partner@tolnigeria.com . For urgent matters, WhatsApp remains the fastest route to a response. Traction Outsourcing Limited continues to build its service offering around what clients actually need, not just what is convenient to deliver. The 24-hour support programme is the latest step in that direction, and the firm expects to expand the channels and team behind it as demand grows. b: Privacy Policy Last updated: July 10, 2026 Traction Outsourcing Limited ("Traction Outsourcing Limited," "we," "us," or "our") respects your privacy. This Privacy Policy explains what information we collect through tolnigeria.com, why we collect it, and how we handle it, in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023 (NDPA) and the General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) issued by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). By using this website, you agree to the practices described here. 1. Information We Collect We collect information in two ways. Information you give us directly. When you fill in a consultation form on this site, we collect your full name, phone number, company name, and email address. If you contact us through WhatsApp, phone, or email instead, we receive whatever information you choose to share in that conversation. Information collected automatically. Like most websites, our hosting provider may log basic technical information such as your browser type and general access times, for security and maintenance purposes. We also use Google Analytics to understand how visitors use this site, such as which pages are viewed and how visitors found us. 2. Lawful Basis & How We Use Your Information We only process your personal data where we have a lawful basis to do so under the NDPA, most commonly your consent (when you voluntarily submit a form) or our legitimate interest in responding to business enquiries. We use the information collected for the following purposes: • To respond to your consultation request and get in touch about our services. • To understand which of our service pages generate enquiries, so we can improve them. • To send you information you have specifically asked for, such as event details or proposals. • To meet legal, regulatory, or contractual obligations where applicable. We do not use your information for automated decision-making, and we do not sell your information to third parties. You may withdraw consent at any time by contacting us, without affecting the lawfulness of any processing carried out before withdrawal. 3. When We Share Information We do not share your information with third parties for marketing purposes. We may share information with trusted service providers who support our business operations (for example, form processing and productivity tools), or where required to do so by Nigerian law, regulation, or a valid legal process. Any third party we work with is expected to handle your information with the same level of care described in this policy. 4. International Data Transfers Some of the service providers that support our operations may process data outside Nigeria. Where this happens, we take reasonable steps to ensure such transfers meet the safeguards required under the NDPA, including relying on providers that maintain adequate data protection standards. 5. Data Security We apply reasonable administrative and technical safeguards to protect your information against unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure, or loss, including restricting access to authorized personnel only. No method of transmission or storage is completely secure, and while we work to protect your information, we cannot guarantee absolute security. In the event of a data breach affecting your personal data, we will take appropriate steps in line with our obligations under the NDPA, including notifying the NDPC and affected individuals where required. 6. Cookies & Tracking This website uses Google Analytics, which places cookies on your device to help us understand how visitors use this site, such as which pages are viewed and how people found us. This data is aggregated and does not identify you personally. We do not use tracking cookies for advertising purposes, and we do not run third-party advertising pixels or share this data with advertisers. You can opt out of Google Analytics tracking using tools such as the Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on, or by adjusting your browser's cookie settings. If our use of cookies or tracking changes in the future, this policy will be updated to reflect it, and where required, you will be asked for consent. 7. Data Retention We keep consultation form submissions for as long as reasonably necessary to respond to your enquiry and maintain business records, or until you ask us to delete it, whichever comes first, in line with the principle of storage limitation under the NDPA. 8. Your Rights Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023, you have the right to: • Know what information we hold about you and how it is processed; • Request a copy of your personal data; • Request a correction if your information is inaccurate or incomplete; • Request that we delete your information, subject to any legal or contractual obligations that require us to keep it; • Object to or request that we restrict certain processing of your data; • Withdraw consent at any time, where processing is based on consent; and • Lodge a complaint directly with us, or with the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), if you believe your data protection rights have been violated. To exercise any of these rights, contact us using the details below. We will respond within the timeframes required under the NDPA. 9. Children's Privacy This website and our services are directed at businesses and adults. We do not knowingly collect information from anyone under the age of 18 without valid parental or guardian consent. 10. Changes To This Policy We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time as our services or applicable law change. The "Last updated" date at the top of this page will reflect the most recent revision. 11. Contact Us & Data Protection Enquiries If you have any questions about this Privacy Policy, wish to exercise any of your data protection rights, or would like to raise a concern about how your information is handled, reach us at: Traction Outsourcing Limited 26, Algiers Street, Wuse Zone 5, FCT, Nigeria Email: partner@tolnigeria.com Phone: 0805 203 3145

b: Books & Resources Books and Resources Featured Book · Leadership Free Nigerian Bosses Are Bad A Short Book on Perspective, Pressure, and the People Who Lead Us Nigerian Bosses Are Bad is a short e-book by Prince Elijah Abumoye, founder of Traction Outsourcing Limited, about why so many bosses in Nigerian workplaces get called wicked, unfair, or impossible to please, and what is really happening underneath that reputation. Written for employees, managers, and business owners across Nigeria, it uses real workplace scenarios rather than management theory to unpack the pressure, structure, and decisions behind difficult leadership, and what changes once a business finally gets those things right. The stories in the book are drawn from patterns Traction Outsourcing has seen firsthand across HR audits, leadership training, and corporate restructuring work inside real Nigerian companies, so the bosses described here will feel familiar rather than invented for effect. Nigerian Bosses Are Bad is available now as a free e-book, and can be downloaded directly from this page. Somewhere in Lagos tonight, somebody is typing a resignation letter at 11 p.m. They will save it in drafts. They will not send it, because rent does not care how you feel about your Oga, and neither does the landlord who is already asking for next quarter before this one has ended. If you have worked under a Nigerian boss, you have said it at least once. Maybe under your breath in the office toilet. Maybe into your phone on the drive home. "This one is wicked." "That woman does not have human blood." "How can somebody treat people like this?" Read a Sample Chapter Two The Boss Who Changes Her Mind Every Monday Tunde had a private nickname for his CEO within six months of joining the fintech in Yaba. He called her NEPA. Her instructions took light like PHCN, here now, gone before you'd finished adjusting to it. The product roadmap that was locked on Monday was scrapped by Wednesday. A payment-processor deal he'd spent three weeks negotiating died two days before signing, killed by a text that said only, it's not the right time anymore. He'd stay up getting a set of wireframes exactly right, proud of the work, and two days later learn none of it would ship. There is a version of this story where Amaka is simply indecisive, a founder who talks a confident game in pitch decks and falls apart the moment a real decision needs holding. That version isn't entirely wrong. It also isn't the whole picture. Amaka runs a fintech company inside a regulatory environment where the Central Bank can issue a circular on a Tuesday morning that makes Monday's entire business model illegal by lunchtime. b: Bank Outsourcing Outsourcing for Banks & Financial Institutions Traction Outsourcing supports banks and financial institutions across Nigeria with outsourced staff for teller operations, customer service, sales, and back-office support, built with the documentation and governance a regulated institution needs. Banks and financial institutions carry a staffing load that most businesses never touch, front-line roles that need to scale with branch expansion, back-office functions that need to run without interruption, and every one of them sitting inside a regulatory environment that does not tolerate loose arrangements. Bringing in a general staffing agency that treats a bank the same as a retail shop rarely holds up. Traction Outsourcing supports banks and financial institutions with outsourced staffing built around that reality, proper documentation, clear service level agreements, and roles managed with the same seriousness the institution applies to its own operations. We are not new to this. We understand what a financial institution actually needs from a staffing partner, and we are positioned to take on more of it. Roles We Place for Banks Front-line, back-office, and support roles, scoped to a single branch or rolled out across many. Tellers & Cash Officers Front-line cash handling and transaction support Customer Service & Contact Center Branch front desk and call center representatives Direct Sales Agents Account opening, card, and loan product sales support Back-Office & Operations Transaction processing and administrative support Loan & Credit Support Documentation and processing support for lending teams Compliance & KYC Support Onboarding documentation and verification support staff IT & Technical Support Branch-level and desk-side technical support Facility, Security & Drivers Branch facility staff, security, and dispatch support Need a role that isn't listed here? Built Around How Banks Actually Operate Outsourcing a function does not outsource accountability for it. Nigerian banks and other CBN-supervised financial institutions are expected to maintain documented risk assessments and governance oversight for any outsourced arrangement, including staffing, as part of their broader risk and cybersecurity framework obligations. Traction Outsourcing structures every bank staffing arrangement with that reality in mind, clear documentation, defined service level agreements, and reporting the institution can actually rely on internally, not a loose staffing arrangement dressed up after the fact. We work quietly and professionally, fitting into how the institution already operates rather than asking it to adapt to us. How It Works The same disciplined process we use across every staffing engagement, scoped to a financial institution's requirements. 1 Diagnose We understand the roles, branch footprint, and governance requirements before proposing anything. 2 Design We build the staffing plan, documentation, and SLAs the institution's risk framework requires. 3 Deploy We place, manage, and report on staff for as long as the arrangement runs, branch by branch if needed. Let's talk about your institution's staffing needs. Why Financial Institutions Work With Us Discretion As Standard Staffing arrangements built to sit inside your institution quietly and professionally, without disruption to how you operate. HR-Certified Leadership Our practice is led by PHRi, SHRM-SCP, and CIPM certified HR professionals, not generalists managing staffing as a side function. Documentation-First Every arrangement is built with the SLAs and reporting your governance framework requires, not added on after the fact. 24/7 Virtual Client Support Reach us at any hour through our round-the-clock support desk, not just during standard business hours. Common Questions Does Traction Outsourcing work with banks in Nigeria? Yes. Traction Outsourcing supports banks and financial institutions in Nigeria with outsourced staff across teller operations, customer service, direct sales, back-office support, and more, managed with the documentation and governance financial institutions require. What roles can a bank outsource through Traction Outsourcing? Common roles include tellers and cash officers, customer service and contact center staff, direct sales agents, back-office and operations support, loan and credit support, compliance and KYC support staff, IT support, and facility and security staff. Is outsourced bank staff still the bank's regulatory responsibility? Yes. Regulatory bodies are clear that outsourcing an operational function does not outsource accountability for it. Banks remain responsible for the outcomes of outsourced roles, which is why every arrangement is built with proper documentation, SLAs, and reporting the institution can rely on. We prepared the full negotiation position, opening terms through to walk-away terms, across eight deal points, and identified bar revenue and beverage control as the highest-margin point worth holding firm on. The clearest signal is when you are making significant decisions without enough information, experience, or objective input to make them well. b: Areas Of Impact Corporate Restructuring Legacy frameworks quietly slow a business down long before anyone names the problem. We name it, then rebuild the structure around where the business actually needs to go. When a Business Needs Restructuring Traction Outsourcing Limited manages every dimension of a restructuring engagement, from governance and organograms through to ownership structures, shareholder matters, and statutory requirements. Growth Has Outpaced Your Structure Reporting lines, roles, and decision-making built for an earlier headcount start breaking under current growth. We rebuild the framework around where the business is now. Two Entities Need to Run as One Group Separate entities with separate histories need a shared governance register, organogram, and policy structure to actually function as a single group. We manage the full process, from the operational rebuild to the ownership restructure, shareholder agreements, and statutory documentation.
